documents.abstract: Ael-Agents is a biomimetic multi-agent coordination architecture modeled on the human triple-network cortical hierarchy—Default Mode Network (DMN), Salience Network (SN), and Central Executive Network (CEN)—coupled with offline Dream-RSI (Recursive Self-Improvement) consolidation, specialized for Computational Drug Discovery and Precision Therapeutics. The architecture segregates the therapeutic pipeline into 4 orthogonal domain specialists (StructuralBiophysics, SystemsPharmacology, MedicinalChemistryADMET, ClinicalPKPDControl). Hypotheses are embedded in a 768-dimensional neural manifold (BAAI/bge-base-en-v1.5) to compute a 4x4 Representational Dissimilarity Matrix (RDM) in the DMN, while exact PyTorch autograd Jacobian sensitivity analysis gates the top k=2 working-memory specialists into executive synthesis for 0 LLM tokens (~2,200 tokens/run, a 93.7% token reduction). Includes a deterministic benchmark suite evaluated via RDKit (valence, Lipinski Rule of 5, QED druglikeness) and SciPy 2-compartment pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic ODE numerical integration on KRAS-G12D, human board-exam pharmacology validation (MedMCQA), and ground-truth human semantic alignment (SimLex-999 rho = +0.5711, STS-Benchmark rho = +0.8642, Monte Carlo RDM stability p = 0.0002).

documents.abstract: This paper presents a conceptual review of Agentic Artificial Intelligence (AI), autonomous agents, and multi-agent system security. It discusses key security threats, including prompt injection, excessive tool permissions, sensitive data leakage, memory poisoning, insecure inter-agent communication, and cascading failures. The paper proposes a layered security framework incorporating identity management, least-privilege access, policy-controlled tool usage, secure agent communication, memory protection, monitoring, bounded autonomy, and human approval for high-impact actions. It also outlines an evaluation methodology using adversarial test cases and measurable security and performance metrics. This work aims to support the development of safer, more reliable, and secure agentic AI systems. The proposed framework is conceptual and literature-based; no prototype implementation or experimental results are claimed.

As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes increasingly integrated into library services, understanding librarians’ psychological responses to this technological transformation has become an important research priority. This study investigates AI anxiety among university librarians in Bangladesh and examines whether anxiety levels vary across demographic and professional characteristics. A cross-sectional survey was conducted using the Artificial Intelligence Anxiety Scale (AIAS). Data were collected from librarians employed in public and private universities in Bangladesh through convenience sampling. Following data-quality screening, 138 valid responses were retained for analysis. Descriptive statistics, reliability analysis, correlation analysis, and one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) with Bonferroni post hoc tests were employed to examine patterns of AI anxiety and group differences. Overall, university librarians reported a moderate level of AI anxiety (M = 3.00). Anxiety levels were broadly comparable across dimensions, although Sociotechnical Blindness recorded a slightly higher mean score than the remaining dimensions. Educational qualification and professional experience showed limited overall associations with AI anxiety, while gender, age, and professional designation demonstrated little variation. The findings suggest that concerns regarding governance, transparency, professional identity, and organizational readiness may be more salient than technological learning challenges. The study extends research on AI anxiety to a Global South library context and contributes evidence that AI anxiety among university librarians is well understood as an interrelated socio-professional and organizational phenomenon. The findings highlight the importance of professional development, institutional support, and responsible AI governance in academic libraries.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) in education has largely been positioned as a child-facing tutor, conversational agent, or content-delivery system. In early childhood, this orientation warrants particular caution because executive functions, self-regulation, and social-emotional competencies develop through responsive relationships, play, embodied experience, and co-regulation with adults. This theory-informed conceptual design study addressed three questions: which developmental, pedagogical, and ethical principles should structure AI use in early childhood; how these principles can be translated into a system architecture; and what validation pathway is required before such a system can make defensible claims. Drawing on four evidence streams (executive-function and social-emotional development, ecological and embodied learning, human-centered AI ethics, and measurement and implementation science), the study proposes the Behind-the-Adult AI framework, an adult-mediated design framework initially specified for children aged 4–6 years. Six design principles were derived and operationalized in a layered architecture: brief, bounded, non-conversational digital developmental tasks generate behavioral indicators under transparent adaptation rules; a provisional, non-diagnostic profile organizes longitudinal information; and AI operates only behind the adult, synthesizing observations from center, home, and school into hypotheses for human review. A five-stage validation pathway with explicit decision gates separates design claims from evidence claims. The paper argues that developmentally responsible AI in early childhood should be evaluated not by how convincingly it replaces human interaction but by how effectively it strengthens the adults and environments surrounding the child, and it offers a transferable design heuristic for researchers, developers, and policymakers.

Universities increasingly use AI content detection tools to identify student assignments potentially produced by generative AI, yet concerns remain regarding their reliability and false-positive classification of human-written work. This systematic review examines the causes, consequences, and mitigation of false-positive AI detection in academic contexts. The review covers literature published between 2020 and 2026 and includes 90 eligible studies, comprising 81 Scopus-indexed publications and nine studies identified through Google Scholar. Bibliometric mapping using VOSviewer was combined with Structural Topic Modelling to examine keyword relationships, latent research themes, and temporal development, while qualitative synthesis identified major causes, impacts, and mitigation strategies. The findings reveal three broader themes concerning academic integrity and student assessment, plagiarism and responsible AI governance, and detection accuracy, reliability, and false positives. False-positive outcomes vary substantially across tools and evaluation settings, limiting direct quantitative comparison. Major contributing factors include algorithmic and language bias, limited contextual understanding, surface-level linguistic features, and insufficiently diverse training data. The evidence further highlights risks to assessment fairness, student confidence, and institutional decision-making. Effective responses therefore require transparent detection practices, human review, AI literacy, clear institutional policies, and accessible appeal procedures.

AI-Assisted Social Science Research: Methods, Governance and Reason Provenance is a practical research and educational resource for documenting and governing generative-AI-assisted social-science research. The resource develops a workflow for distinguishing AI-assisted proposal generation, researcher evaluation and governance, local empirical execution, adversarial challenge, manuscript revision and reason provenance. It includes reusable templates, completed worked examples drawn from the PISA research programme, guidance on claim preservation and manuscript governance, and public-release screening materials. The resource is intended to support transparent attribution and disciplined research practice rather than to prescribe a universal workflow or to provide evidence that AI-assisted research is inherently superior to human-only research.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: This research paper presents an AI-based framework for predicting the State of Health (SOH) of electric vehicle (EV) lithium-ion batteries by integrating machine learning, Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI), and relational database technology. The proposed framework compares five machine learning regression models: Ridge Regression, Support Vector Regression (SVR), Multilayer Perceptron (MLP), Random Forest, and Gradient Boosting. SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) are used to explain model predictions and identify important battery health indicators, including dV/dQ peak height, internal resistance, and cycle count. The study demonstrates the proposed pipeline using a synthetic, physics-inspired dataset containing 40 battery cells and 28,201 cycle records. Gradient Boosting achieved a Mean Absolute Error (MAE) of 1.26 percentage points, a Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE) of 1.70 percentage points, and an R² score of 0.967 on the held-out synthetic test cells. An SQLite database stores battery information, cycle data, predictions, explanations, and alerts. The framework aims to improve the interpretability, traceability, and management of EV battery health predictions. However, the reported results are based entirely on synthetic data and do not establish real-world battery prediction accuracy. Future work includes validation using public battery datasets, such as NASA and CALCE, and further evaluation under real-world conditions.

AI-Based Traffic Flow Optimization System Using Computer Vision: Research Design and Prototype Abstract Urban traffic congestion contributes to increased travel time, fuel consumption, and road-safety challenges. Conventional fixed-time traffic signal systems may not respond efficiently to changing traffic demand. This project presents the design of an AI-based traffic flow optimization system using computer vision to support traffic monitoring, vehicle detection, traffic density estimation, vehicle tracking, and adaptive traffic signal recommendations. Objectives The primary objectives are to: Detect and count vehicles from traffic video footage using computer vision. Estimate traffic density across different approaches at an intersection. Analyze traffic conditions to identify congestion and potential incidents. Develop a density-aware signal allocation approach that responds to changing traffic demand. Explore emergency vehicle prioritization and traffic-performance evaluation. Methodology The proposed system integrates computer vision, vehicle detection, tracking, traffic density analysis, and signal optimization into a unified monitoring framework. Traffic observations are processed to estimate vehicle counts and congestion levels. These estimates can inform signal-duration recommendations, subject to appropriate operational and safety constraints. The research workflow also includes dataset inspection, data cleaning, source documentation, and an experimental comparison framework. Potential evaluation metrics include vehicle-counting accuracy, average waiting time, queue length, throughput, and fairness across traffic approaches. Research Contribution The project provides an integrated prototype for investigating computer-vision-based traffic management. Its contribution lies in combining traffic observation, density analysis, adaptive signal recommendations, and research-oriented data-quality tools within a single system. The framework is intended to support further experimentation and reproducible evaluation of intelligent transportation approaches. Data Sources and Limitations Official road-safety statistics from published government sources are used to provide historical context for Jaipur and Rajasthan, with geographic scope identified separately. The demonstration intersection dataset contains synthetic records for testing the data-processing workflow; it is not a collection of measured Jaipur traffic observations. The current prototype does not establish experimentally validated reductions in real-world waiting time, congestion, fuel consumption, or emissions. Such claims require verified traffic observations, documented experimental conditions, and controlled comparisons against a fixed-time baseline. Future Scope Future work includes collecting authorized traffic-video observations from selected Jaipur intersections, validating vehicle-detection accuracy against manually annotated samples, evaluating signal-allocation strategies under comparable demand conditions, and reporting statistical uncertainty and limitations. Keywords Computer Vision; Intelligent Transportation Systems; Traffic Flow Optimization; Vehicle Detection; Vehicle Tracking; Traffic Density Estimation; Adaptive Traffic Signal Control; Road Safety; Jaipur; Artificial Intelligence.

Educational institutions influence environmental responsibility through teaching, leadership, resource use, and the decisions that shape everyday campus life. Artificial intelligence introduces additional opportunities and responsibilities within these activities. This chapter develops a conceptual account of AI-enabled institutional governance that connects ethical leadership, sustainability education, and accountable administrative practice. It uses a narrative synthesis of established educational theories, published environmental education reviews, and primary international guidance on education, AI ethics, and risk management. It does not report an original systematic search, institutional dataset, AI deployment, or intervention evaluation. A published meta-analysis of environmental education among children and adolescents provides contextual evidence of positive average effects on knowledge, attitudes, intentions, and behaviour; these findings do not establish the effectiveness of AI governance in higher education. Digital education research is similarly treated as adjacent evidence rather than proof of an AI-specific benefit. The proposed framework assigns human responsibility across the identification, assessment, operation, and review of institutional AI applications. Examples include curriculum support, student assistance, resource planning, and sustainability communication. Decision boundaries, privacy, fairness, participation, contestability, and teacher capacity are considered alongside environmental objectives. The chapter argues that knowledge and technological capability require supportive institutional conditions before they can contribute to responsible action. It recommends limited pilots with explicit purposes, proportionate data collection, accessible human review, and evaluation against educational and environmental outcomes. The framework remains a proposal requiring contextual adaptation and empirical assessment. It offers educational leaders a basis for connecting sustainability commitments with the governance of AI without assuming that automation itself produces ethical or environmental improvement.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Abstract Large Language Models (LLMs) may support clinicians by facilitating information management, but their usability in real-world oncology practice remains understudied. This study evaluated the workflow performance of Artificial Intelligence-based First Consultation Preparation (AI-FCP), generating structured summaries from unstructured clinical documentation, co-created with end users. In a prospective single‑group pre‑post design, nine clinicians completed a person-level baseline, followed by 33 consultations with AI-FCP. Case numbers varied by clinic scheduling and enrollment timing, potentially introducing survivorship bias. Usability was evaluated using validated questionnaires and study-specific instruments. Post AI-FCP, overall perceived workload (NASA-TLX) was 28.9% lower than baseline (Hodges-Lehmann estimate difference −12.3; 95% CI –21.7 to –3.3), with self-reported average time savings of 3.26 min (SD = 2.65) per case. Preparation succeeded in 84.9% of consultations; 63.6% of summaries were complete. These exploratory findings suggest clinicians perceived lower workload and reported improved workflow efficiency with AI-FCP. Further research is needed to determine generalizability.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: This study develops a jurisprudential, algorithmic, and systems framework for automated regulatory intelligence within the structurally fragmented administrative environment of the United States. Mechanical and HVAC regulation is used as a test domain because a single field operation may simultaneously implicate federal environmental rules, state licensing regimes, county or municipal permitting, locally adopted building codes, technician credentials, and address-specific inspection procedures. Comparative analysis of Illinois, Texas, North Carolina, and Arizona therefore treats the United States not merely as a geographical setting, but as an empirical governance laboratory for examining how artificial intelligence can mediate rules that vary by authority, location, and time. The analysis addresses three related problems. First, Home Rule, Dillon's Rule, and state preemption distribute local regulatory authority differently across the four states, creating materially different operational pathways (Baker & Rodriguez, 2009; Briffault, 2018; Briffault et al., 2020; Diller, 2017; Mead, 2019; Richardson, 2011; Stahl, 2024). Second, the federal HFC phasedown and EPA Technology Transitions program interact with state and local code-adoption cycles; this interaction may create sequencing gaps or administrative uncertainty, but it should not be characterized as a universal direct conflict or as a federal mandate to use one specific A2L refrigerant (U.S. EPA, 2026a, 2026b). Third, digitally generated compliance records require provenance, temporal reconstruction, qualified certification, and notice procedures if they are later offered under Federal Rules of Evidence 901 or 902(13)/(14); cryptographic hashing alone does not establish admissibility (Krishnamurthy, 2025; U.S. Courts, 2017). By combining constitutional and administrative analysis, point-in-polygon jurisdictional resolution, temporal knowledge graphs, constrained generative AI, human-in-the-loop governance, and cryptographic provenance, the study proposes a scalable research architecture rather than claiming a completed production platform. The U.S. HVAC case also provides a bridge to Metaverse governance: it demonstrates how physical territory can first become machine-readable, then algorithmically mediated, and comparable to an electronic jurisdiction in which digital space, identity, activity, and time determine the applicable governance regime (Kostenko et al., 2022, 2024, 2025).

PURPOSE Ambient artificial intelligence (AI) scribes, widely implemented to reduce clinician burden and dissatisfaction, are not optimized for oncology. We evaluated this technology at-scale at a high-volume cancer center. METHODS This prospective mixed-methods study used surveys, electronic health record (EHR), and utilization data to assess adoption, burden, and satisfaction with an ambient AI scribe that was implemented from June to September 2025. Descriptive statistics categorized clinicians as adopters (3+ weeks of use), attempted adopters (1-2 weeks), and never-users (0 weeks). Generalized estimating equations assessed the adoption's effect on the likelihood of closing notes on visit days and pajama time. Pre- and postimplementation surveys obtained clinicians' insights into satisfaction and documentation burden. RESULTS In all, 190 (19.8%) of 958 clinicians used the tool, most often with new, video, and in-person visits. Adopters (n = 124) and attempted adopters (n = 66) were more commonly physicians from medicine and surgery. Pre- to post-rollout, the likelihood of closing notes on visit days remained unchanged among never-users (70% v 70%) and decreased among attempted adopters (73% v 70%) and adopters (56% v 54%). Pajama time remained unchanged among attempted adopters (50.6 v 50.1 minutes per week) and decreased among never-users (69.5 v 62.2) and adopters (86.9 v 81.4). Clinicians completing both pre- and postrollout surveys (n = 45) showed a decrease in high/excessive note-writing time (78% v 60%; P = .043). Postrollout surveys (n = 77) showed largely positive experiences, with 73% reporting they would recommend the tool to colleagues. CONCLUSION This study of an ambient AI scribe at-scale showed positive satisfaction but mixed burden outcomes among oncology clinicians. Notably, despite enterprise-wide implementation and training, adoption was low and varied by clinician and visit characteristics. Future research should explore adoption barriers and tool optimization to support oncology documentation workflows.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) systems increasingly support decisions in environments where data distributions, operational conditions, user needs, and risk levels change over time. Models that perform well during development may become unreliable after deployment because of data drift, concept drift, sensor degradation, population changes, or unexpected interactions. At the same time, predictive performance alone is insufficient for high-impact decisions: users need explanations that are understandable, relevant to the decision context, and accompanied by appropriate uncertainty information. This paper proposes an Adaptive Explainable AI (A-XAI) framework intended to integrate reliability monitoring, explanation generation, uncertainty estimation, human oversight, and controlled model adaptation within a unified lifecycle. The framework contains nine conceptual components: contextual data acquisition; data-quality, privacy, and drift assessment; prediction with uncertainty estimation; context-sensitive explanation generation; decision support and human oversight; risk-aware reliability gating; feedback and audit logging; controlled adaptation; and post-adaptation revalidation with version control. A formal decision policy is presented to connect predictive confidence, drift evidence, explanation quality, and consequence severity to actions such as automated recommendation, human review, abstention, or retraining. The paper also proposes an evaluation protocol spanning predictive performance, calibration, robustness, explanation fidelity and stability, fairness, latency, and operational outcomes. As a conceptual contribution, the framework is not presented as experimentally validated; its effectiveness must be tested in domain-specific studies using real deployment data and preregistered evaluation criteria. The proposed design offers a structured basis for developing AI systems that remain interpretable and risk-aware as real-world conditions evolve.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: This study proposes a fully automated exam marking framework for English writing in the General Foundation Program (GFP) through the use of prompt engineering with artificial intelligence (AI) tool ChatGPT and computer-based analysis. The AI tool generated 120 GFP B2 level writing responses (120 to 150 words each) with intentional grammatical errors. Four prompts were applied for automated marking by the AI tool as an examiner, based on a provided rubric, to detect errors, and awarding of a score [/10] (out of 10) to each response. A combination of different prompting techniques, including instruction-based, role-based, and formatting prompting were collectively used to design each prompt. All of the 120 responses were marked by each prompt. The first and second prompts were similar, just with a difference of paraphrasing. Prompts 3 and 4 were based on Prompt 2, containing only an addition of a single word for Prompt 3, and replacement of the added word with another word for Prompt 4. Statistical comparisons were done in SPSS. The Friedman test showed the similarities (Prompts 1 and 2 with paraphrased versions) and significant differences (Prompts 2, 3 and 4; p < .001, just due to an addition, and replacement of a single word) among the prompts outcomes based on the markings. Pairwise comparisons were performed using the Bonferroni correction to check for significant differences, while Kendall’s W test was used to measure the strength of agreement among the rankings. Human involvement in the study was limited to author-led validation of all the 120 responses, toward the accuracy of intentional added errors. The framework demonstrated how different prompts impacted the marking outcomes, which highlighted the sensitivity of the prompts to the addition of a single determinative word and the replacement of that word with another. Moreover, statistical comparisons showed how scalable assessment design and quality checks can be consistently applied for GFP English writing. This study showed that the proposed automated marking framework can support consistent, scalable, and prompt-sensitive assessment of GFP English writing.

Can a robot's ethical reasoning be transparent without slowing it down? That is the question we set out to answer. Autonomous robots now make decisions that affect people's lives, and if we cannot understand how they decide, trust becomes a serious problem. We built a unified architecture that couples Explainable AI (XAI) with Reinforcement Learning (RL) through three connected components: a Perception Layer for situational awareness, a Decision Reasoning Layer that breaks agent utility down into measurable ethical sub-rewards (safety, fairness, and well-being), and a contrastive Explainability Engine grounded in a real-time Ethical Ledger. We tested it against Black-Box RL and two post-hoc XRL baselines (LIME and SHAP) across two simulation environments and a physical robot pilot on a TurtleBot3 platform. Our system reached 92±3% ethical alignment in simulation and 89±4% on the physical platform, beating every baseline (p < 0.01 throughout). In a controlled, IRB-approved user study (N=128), participants rated it higher on trust (4.5±0.4), understandability (4.6±0.3), and perceived safety (4.4±0.5) than the alternatives. Explanations were also fast: 4.2±0.6 ms on average, versus 18.3±2.1 ms for SHAP and 12.7±1.8 ms for LIME on the same hardware—well within real-time limits. An ablation study and sensitivity analysis back up these architectural choices.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Hand-based gestures are widely used in human-computer interaction but can cause muscle fatigue and discomfort that undermine long-term usability. This exploratory study examined whether gestures' ease of use can be reflected in distinct muscle activation patterns derived from surface electromyography (sEMG) signals. Twenty participants performed 32 predefined gestures while sEMG was recorded from eight forearm and upper-arm muscles, and rated each gesture's perceived effort on a 7-point scale. Gestures were grouped into high- and low-ease-of-use categories, and activation features were compared between groups. Results showed that high-ease-of-use gestures had significantly greater biceps activation, lower extensor carpi radialis activation, and reduced co-activation between the flexor carpi ulnaris and flexor digitorum superficialis. These findings suggest that ease of use relates to reduced motor complexity and reliance on proximal muscles, and demonstrate promise for sEMG in objectively indexing gestures' ease of use, offering insights to inform the design of more usable gesture-based interactions.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) is becoming an increasingly visible part of the modern media environment. Its role is no longer limited to automated or computational journalism; it is now being explored across several stages of media production, including content writing, editing, transcription, translation, fact-checking, audience analysis, recommendation, and personalization. As generative AI and large language models have developed, academic interest in their use within journalism and media organizations has also increased considerably. Recent studies and reviews show that research in this area has expanded from early discussions of automated journalism to broader questions concerning how AI is changing newsroom practices and professional work. This review examines existing research on AI adoption in media organizations, focusing particularly on changes in newsroom practices, organizational processes, journalistic roles, editorial decision-making, and the social and cultural dimensions of AI use. The paper brings together earlier research on automated and algorithmic journalism with more recent literature on generative AI, journalist–AI collaboration, newsroom implementation, ethical concerns, and organizational barriers. The literature suggests that AI can help media organizations handle repetitive and data-intensive tasks more efficiently, allowing journalists to devote greater attention to activities that require interpretation and editorial judgement. However, the growing use of AI also raises important concerns about human oversight, algorithmic transparency, accountability, professional autonomy, and the quality and context of media content. Particular attention is given to India and other countries of the Global South, where the adoption of AI takes place within different economic, organizational, linguistic, and cultural settings. Research from these contexts indicates that AI adoption is developing, but its implementation is not always uniform. Limited resources, inadequate training, organizational preparedness, and the absence of clear ethical guidelines can influence how effectively media organizations integrate AI into their professional practices. Overall, the review suggests that AI adoption in media should not be understood simply as a technological shift aimed at improving speed and efficiency. It is also influencing the nature of journalistic work, editorial responsibility, and the relationship between media organizations and the communities they serve. Therefore, understanding AI adoption requires attention not only to its operational benefits but also to its implications for the social and cultural responsibilities of media.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: This study critically examines the relationship between Artificial Intelligence and copyright law by focusing on the three foundational concepts of authorship, ownership, and originality. It evaluates existing legal frameworks, judicial decisions, international developments, and scholarly opinions to determine whether current copyright principles are capable of addressing AI-generated works or whether legislative reform is required, and proposes recommendations aimed at balancing technological advancement with the protection of human creativity.

ABSTRACTThis thorough analysis examines the revolutionary significance of artificial intelligence (AI)in contemporary healthcare, stressing its development, uses, difficulties, and legalconsiderations. From its initial limits, artificial intelligence has quickly advanced to providesophisticated features like deep learning and predictive analytics. It is transformingmedication discovery, rehabilitation, treatment planning, diagnostics, and healthcaremanagement. Patient care is becoming more accurate, efficient, and personalized thanks toapplications like data-driven decision support systems, virtual care, and AI-enhancedimaging.

documents.abstract: This article is a systematic review of previously published, peer-reviewed studies; no participant-level or confidential data were generated. All materials underpinning the review are openly available in the Zenodo repository at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23429519 under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0) licence. The repository includes the complete search strategies, the screening and exclusion logs, the data-extraction and coding materials, the coding frameworks, the Severity, Effectiveness, ESI, and RRW scoring rubrics, and the analytic audit-trail documentation. The full texts of the included studies are not redistributed because they are copyrighted publications; they are available from their original publishers.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly influencing pharmaceutical manufacturing and quality management by enabling data-driven process monitoring, prediction, automation, and decision support. This narrative review examines the application of AI across major pharmaceutical manufacturing operations and within quality assurance (QA) and quality control (QC). The review focuses on machine learning, deep learning, computer vision, natural language processing, predictive analytics, Internet of Things (IoT)-enabled monitoring, robotics, and digital-twin technologies. Potential applications include raw-material inspection, dispensing and weighing, granulation, blending, tablet compression, capsule filling, coating, packaging, warehouse management, predictive maintenance, documentation review, deviation management, corrective and preventive action (CAPA), validation support, risk assessment, visual inspection, laboratorydata interpretation, stability studies, and process analytical technology (PAT). AI can improve speed, consistency, traceability, and early detection of process or quality problems; however, these benefits depend on data quality, appropriate validation, cybersecurity, system integration, human oversight, and regulatory acceptability. Current regulatory activity, including the U.S. Food and Drug Administration's discussion paper on AI in drug manufacturing, demonstrates the growing importance of risk-based approaches to AI adoption. Overall, AI should be viewed as an enabling technology that augments, rather than replaces, pharmaceutical professionals. Responsible implementation combining validated digital systems with human expertise may support safer, more efficient, and more reliable pharmaceutical manufacturing.

documents.abstract: This study develops a framework explaining how artificial intelligence (AI) reconfigures customer experience in hospitality and tourism, drawing on service-dominant logic. Co-citation and content analyses were conducted to synthesize 89 articles and identify the intellectual structure of the literature. The findings reveal that institutional arrangements condition AI's legitimate participation in service ecosystems. Three mechanisms explain how AI reconfigures customer experience: the actor role architect, the interaction mediator, and the experience orchestrator. These mechanisms operate concurrently and recursively rather than as discrete stages within AI-enabled service ecosystems. The study makes three contributions to the literature. First, it positions customer experience reconfiguration as an ecosystem-level process. Second, it extends service-dominant logic from dyadic to triadic human-AI-human value co-creation. Third, it differentiates AI by functional intelligence, showing that mechanical, thinking, feeling, and multi-functional types perform distinct roles in this reconfiguration.

Artificial intelligence (AI) changes the conditions under which universities generate knowledge, organise teaching, evaluate individual achievement and justify academic awards. Its significance is not exhausted by the efficiency of automated tools or the detection of misconduct: AI unsettles the relationship among intended competence, performed intellectual work, submitted evidence and accountable educational judgement. This chapter develops a Rwanda-anchored, critically evidence-based account of responsible AI integration across curriculum, pedagogy, assessment, institutional management and external review. A purposive documentary and conceptual synthesis combines foundational scholarship, recent experimental research syntheses on learning outcomes and assessment validity with UNESCO guidance, the National AI Policy, Rwanda's data-protection law, Higher Education Council instruments and international risk-management benchmarks. It differentiates generative, predictive, adaptive and increasingly agentic applications; examines disciplinary and role-specific AI literacy; and analyses authorship, academic integrity, accessibility, bias, privacy, procurement, academic labour and technological dependence. The chapter's distinctive contribution is an evidence-traceable governance model connecting educational purpose, legitimate authority, bounded AI use, independently interpretable assessment evidence, learner protection and reviewable decisions. Practical instruments include an institutional AI governance and academic assessment integrity framework, task-level disclosure template, assessment-redesign matrix, risk-based tool appraisal and worked hypothetical evaluation. These are original professional proposals, not regulator-approved or independently validated instruments. The chapter concludes that trustworthy AI-enabled higher education requires greater, rather than diminished, human responsibility for what is taught, learned, assessed and certified.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Purpose: Artificial intelligence (AI) is now embedded in teaching, assessment and administration in higher education, simultaneously widening educational opportunity and institutional cyber exposure. This review examines how AI-related and conventional cyber threats affect the continuity of digital learning, how AI can both amplify and mitigate those threats, and which integrated responses are feasible for resource-constrained universities, with Nigeria as the illustrative context. Design/Methodology/Approach: A narrative integrative review following established integrative-review guidance synthesised 60 sources published mainly between 2019 and 2026, comprising peer-reviewed studies, technical standards, policy and legal instruments, and institutional or industry reports. Sources were organised by threat mechanism, institutional vulnerability, educational consequence, response and implementation constraint, and each was classified by the type of inference it can support. Findings: Seven overlapping threat clusters were identified: AI-enhanced social engineering and identity abuse; ransomware and extortion; privacy leakage and surveillance; platform and supply-chain compromise; manipulation of AI-enabled learning systems; synthetic media and assessment-integrity attacks; and human, governance and infrastructure weaknesses. Experimental evidence shows that large language models lower the cost of persuasive phishing, while AI-text detectors and automated proctoring raise reliability and fairness concerns. AI-assisted defence offers measurable triage benefits but introduces false alarms, concept drift, privacy exposure and automation bias. Originality/Value: The proposed AI-Cybersecurity-Digital Learning Resilience (AIC-DLR) Framework adapts NIST CSF 2.0 functions to the educational mission, overlays NIST AI risk-management guidance, and treats usable, equitable recovery of teaching and assessment, rather than system restoration alone, as the protected outcome. A tiered roadmap and a set of operationally defined indicators translate the framework into testable practice. Practical Implications: Priorities for low-capacity institutions are accountable ownership, phishing-resistant identity for privileged users, tested and isolated backups, proportionate data practices, governed AI use and pre-authorised alternative learning channels. The framework is conceptual and unvalidated; comparative implementation studies are required to establish its effect on recovery time and equitable access.

Abstract Artificial intelligence has moved from the margins of human resource management into its everyday machinery. Applicant tracking systems now rank candidates, chatbots answer policy questions, predictive models flag employees likely to resign, and large language models draft job descriptions and appraisal summaries. Research has grown quickly alongside this adoption, but it remains scattered across human resource management, information systems, operations research and computer science, and the regional scholarship published outside English-language journals is rarely integrated into it. This article reports a systematic review of 82 peer-reviewed studies published between January 2015 and March 2026, retrieved from Scopus, Web of Science, EBSCO Business Source Complete, ScienceDirect and the Russian scientific database eLIBRARY.RU, and screened following PRISMA 2020 guidance. Thematic synthesis produced six themes: recruitment and selection; learning, development and internal mobility; performance management and predictive analytics; employee experience and generative AI; determinants of adoption; and fairness, transparency and governance. Three findings stand out. First, the evidence base is heavily skewed towards recruitment, which accounts for roughly two in five studies, while compensation, industrial relations and occupational safety are barely represented. Second, reported benefits are concentrated in process efficiency, which is comparatively easy to measure, whereas claims about decision quality rest on weaker designs and shorter time horizons. Third, adoption failure is more often organisational than technical: the recurring constraints are data quality, scarce analytical skill inside the HR function, and the absence of an internal governance routine. We argue that value from AI in human resource management depends on treating it as an organisational capability rather than a procurement decision, and we set out a research agenda addressing longitudinal outcome measurement, employee justice perceptions, and evidence from emerging and transition economies. Keywords Artificial intelligence; human resource management; HR information systems; algorithmic decision-making; people analytics; systematic literature review; AI governance; algorithmic fairness

documents.abstract: The research measured the readiness of faculty and students of higher education institutions (HEIs) in Chhattisgarh, India in terms of five dimensions: awareness of AI, technical skills, digital infrastructure, policy and institutional support, and attitude toward AI. The data was collected from four types of institutions, through a cross-sectional survey design with the help of stratified sampling technique with 440 respondents consisting of 120 faculty members and 320 students. An overall Artificial Intelligence Readiness Index (ARI) was calculated using a 5-point scale. Readiness was moderate (M = 3.24, SD = 0.45): attitude and awareness and infrastructure and institutional policy were the highest and the lowest scores respectively. Students performed significantly higher than faculty on the ARI, t (205) = 5.41, p < .001, and the readiness differed by institution type, F(3, 436) = 16.0, p < .001, with government colleges being the lowest. The results showed that 62.7% of the variance of attitude towards AI could be accounted for by awareness, skills, infrastructure and policy support. The results highlight an infrastructure-governance gap as a more likely cause than a motivation gap, and suggestions are provided on paths forward for state policymakers and institutional leaders. Note: The data analysed in this draft are illustrative (simulated) and must be replaced by actual survey responses prior to submission and/or publication.

documents.abstract: This pilot study investigated prefrontal cortex (PFC) activation during a mental arithmetic task in a virtual reality (VR) environment, using functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) to assess cognitive engagement. Seven university students completed a relaxation phase followed by a VR-based arithmetic task while brain activity was recorded using a 16-optode continuous-wave fNIRS system. Oxygenation levels were compared between relaxation and task phases across four PFC subregions using paired t-tests. The left dorsolateral PFC (DLPFC) showed significantly higher oxygenation during the math task compared to relaxation ( p = .026). Other regions exhibited similar but nonsignificant trends. These patterns are consistent with prior real-world fNIRS studies on mental arithmetic. The findings support the feasibility of combining fNIRS with VR for cognitive engagement research in educational and human factors contexts.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping marketing and consumer-brand interactions through personalization, efficiency, prediction, and scalability. Its expanding role, however, raises a more fundamental question: what does AI add to consumer interactions, and where does human involvement remain especially valuable? Using signaling theory as its principal explanatory lens, this chapter develops the concept of augmented brand intelligence to explain how human and artificial intelligence can function as complementary sources of brand signals in consumer-facing interactions. A structured critical synthesis of research on AI in marketing, human-AI collaboration, consumer responses to AI, signaling, and consumer-brand relationships suggests that human involvement can signal relational capability through empathy, contextual judgment, relational understanding, and authentic engagement, whereas AI can signal technological capability through efficiency, personalization, analytical capability, and innovation. The framework distinguishes signal complementarity from signal congruence: complementarity concerns whether human and AI signals contribute distinct, nonredundant information about the brand or the capabilities it offers, whereas congruence concerns whether those signals convey compatible meanings about the brand. Complementary signals are expected to reduce perceived information asymmetry more strongly when congruence is high, because consumers can integrate distinct information into a coherent interpretation of the brand. The framework is illustrated across five application domains: customer service, personalization, brand communication, recommendation systems, and customer relationship management. By moving beyond a substitution-focused perspective, the chapter explains how the orchestration of human and AI capabilities can create credible, trusted, and relationally meaningful consumer experiences, and concludes with managerial guidance and an agenda for empirical research across diverse consumer, brand, and technological contexts.

documents.abstract: This research paper presents a proposed framework for Autonomous AI Agents for Software Development, focusing on the transition from code generation to automated testing, debugging, and software verification. The paper introduces a modular, role-based architecture consisting of a planner agent, context retriever, coder agent, tester agent, debugger agent, and reviewer agent. These components work together through a bounded Plan-Code-Test-Repair workflow to understand software requirements, retrieve relevant code, generate changes, execute tests, diagnose failures, and improve code quality. The proposed framework emphasizes functional correctness, automated test generation, repository-level issue resolution, secure tool execution, human approval, and auditability. It also outlines an evaluation protocol using established benchmarks and metrics to assess code correctness, test quality, efficiency, cost, reliability, and security. This work synthesizes existing research on large language models, reasoning-and-acting agents, self-debugging, multi-agent systems, and automated software testing. It provides a conceptual architecture and evaluation plan for future implementation and experimentation. No implemented system or benchmark results are claimed in this paper. The research aims to support the development of more reliable, secure, and transparent AI-assisted software engineering systems.

Passive neck-support exoskeletons may reduce surgical physical workload, but conventional summaries of the entire task may not catch when these benefits emerge and how muscle activity and posture evolve together. This study evaluated a passive neck-support exoskeleton during 36 live veterinary surgeries performed by 10 surgeons using EMG and IMU measures. Statistical analyses included linear mixed models for task-average EMG and IMU outcomes, generalized additive mixed models for time-varying intervention effects, and lagged cross-correlation analyses for EMG-IMU temporal coupling. The exoskeleton significantly reduced the neck range of motion. Temporal analyses showed delayed reductions in upper trapezius activation, with decreases during the middle-to-late phase of surgery, and direction-specific changes in head-neck kinematics. Coupling analysis showed stronger %MVE-posture coupling in the control condition, but stronger MPF-posture coupling under intervention. These findings suggest that passive neck support may reduce muscle loading and alter fatigue-related muscle-posture coordination during prolonged surgical work.

The rapid integration of artificial intelligence (AI) in education has reshaped instructional practices, making teachers’ readiness and confidence critical considerations. This study determined the level of Grade 7 teachers’ behavioral intention towards AI integration and self-efficacy. Specifically, it described the respondents’ profile in terms of age, sex, position, educational attainment, and AI-related training; their behavioral intention based on attitude, subjective norm, and perceived behavioral control; their self-efficacy concerning student engagement, instructional strategy, and classroom management; the relationship between the two variables; and whether respondents’ profile moderates this relationship. A quantitative descriptive-correlational design was employed, involving 185 Grade 7 teachers from the districts of Kadingilan, Damulog, Kibawe, and Dangcagan in the Division of Bukidnon, selected through universal sampling. Data were gathered using a researcher-made questionnaire. Mean, standard deviation, Pearson Product-Moment Correlation, and multiple linear regression were used for statistical treatment. Findings revealed a very high level of behavioral intention and self-efficacy among teachers, with a significant positive relationship between the two variables, further moderated by respondents’ profile, particularly position and trainings attended. The study concludes that teachers’ favorable behavioral intention toward AI strengthens their self-efficacy. It is recommended that school heads may enhance teachers’ readiness and confidence in integrating AI into instruction.

documents.abstract: Fine jewelry retailers must reconcile uncertain demand, high-value inventory, complex material histories, and expectations of responsible sourcing. This article develops a responsible artificial intelligence framework that connects demand forecasting, provenance evidence, and governance within retail planning. A conceptual framework-development approach informed by design-science research combines a targeted literature update through October 9, 2026, with descriptive analysis of published market statistics and an external retail forecasting benchmark. The analysis distinguishes original design propositions from empirical findings reported by other researchers; no retailer-level experiment or environmental impact assessment was conducted. Three sourced bar charts illustrate changing gold jewelry consumption and the methodological relevance of inventory-based model evaluation. The resulting architecture integrates data inputs, predictive analytics, provenance and traceability, ethical governance, and human-reviewed decisions with feedback. Five design principles and five testable propositions specify how forecasts can inform assortment, replenishment, allocation, and sourcing while preserving evidence quality and accountability. The framework shifts evaluation from forecast accuracy alone toward decision quality under explicit operational and provenance constraints. It also separates inventory efficiency, sourcing documentation, and environmental outcomes, preventing improvements in one category from being misrepresented as proof of another. Managerial implications include staged implementation, evidence-qualified sourcing rules, meaningful review authority, and documented overrides. Future validation should compare complete decision policies, preserve temporal information boundaries, measure calibrated reliance, and assess environmental consequences independently. The article contributes a sector-specific architecture and evaluation agenda for accountable retail intelligence without claiming that the integrated framework has already demonstrated operational or sustainability benefits across fine jewelry businesses and markets.

documents.abstract: OBJECTIVES: Artificial intelligence-assisted systems increasingly produce personalized meal plans, but their value depends on whether clinicians judge those plans credible and usable. We evaluated complete plans from a constrained artificial intelligence-assisted pipeline under blinded professional review. METHODS: In a cross-sectional exploratory web study, 54 eligible anonymous evaluator records from Brazilian dietitians contributed 130 evaluations of five matched plan pairs, with one pipeline-generated and one dietitian-designed plan per persona. Evaluators rated nine items across three domains and were offered an optional pairwise plan preference task. The overall score required all nine items and was available for 124 evaluations. RESULTS: Pipeline-generated plans received a mean rating of 3.67 (standard deviation, 0.57) (n = 59) compared with 3.11 (standard deviation, 0.73) for comparator plans (n = 65) (d = 0.86). Among 38 evaluator records with complete scores for both origins, 31 favored pipeline-generated plans, 6 favored dietitian-designed plans, and 1 had equal mean scores for both origins (paired t[37] = 5.32, P < 0.001). Pipeline-generated plans received higher ratings in all five persona pairs. This pattern was descriptive because evaluator records overlapped across pairs. Domain differences were +0.76 for nutritional adequacy, +0.69 for technical quality, and +0.21 for practical applicability. In the optional task, 32 of 42 eligible pairwise choices selected the pipeline-generated plan as more appropriate. CONCLUSIONS: Under blinded presentation, practicing dietitians gave plans from the constrained pipeline a mean rating above the neutral anchor of the 5-point scale. These findings support prospective evaluation of a structured first draft workflow, with required clinician edits and patient-relevant outcomes as endpoints.

documents.abstract: Flow is a deeply immersive psychological state characterized by intense concentration, intrinsic motivation, and a perceived balance between challenge and skill. Although prior research has examined flow in contexts such as sports, education, and workplace performance, limited attention has been paid to how social, cognitive, and motivational factors are associated with flow experiences among practicing artists. This study examined the relationships among perceived social support, the positive mindset dimension, creative process, expected self/life, and flow among practicing artists in China. Drawing on a sample of 962 artists, the study employed Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) to assess theoretically informed associations among social support from friends, family, and significant others, internal psychological factors, and flow experiences. The findings showed that creative process and expected self/life were positively associated with flow-related experiences, whereas the positive mindset dimension was not directly associated with flow. Social support was also associated with internal psychological factors relevant to creative engagement. Mediation analyses indicated that creative process and expected self/life were significant indirect pathways linking the positive mindset dimension and flow. The model demonstrated satisfactory explanatory and predictive relevance, supporting the integration of social and psychological correlates in understanding flow among artistic populations. These findings highlight the relevance of supportive social environments and internal psychological resources in relation to creative engagement and flow, while acknowledging that the cross-sectional and self-report design does not permit causal or temporal conclusions.

As conversational artificial intelligence models become ubiquitous fixtures in professional and personal workflows, the nature of human-tool interaction has the potential to gradually shift from mechanical utility to parasocial dependency. While existing literature frequently addresses adverse events related to data privacy, algorithmic bias, and intellectual deskilling, the pathopsychological sequelae of sustained AI integration remain largely unexamined. Here, we describe and preliminarily characterize the AI Assistant Syndrome, a human psychiatric construct encompassing acute chatbot-induced anxiety and mental exhaustion. This preliminary description will guide future systematic investigations to recognize, prevent, and treat this syndrome.

documents.abstract: Coal mine safety risk assessment can reduce accidents, but traditional methods rely on subjective expert judgment or isolated sensor monitoring, which cannot assess complex and interrelated diverse security risks. This paper proposes a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) framework based on causal reasoning knowledge subgraphs. We first construct a coal mine safety knowledge graph that integrates risk factors, solutions, and legal bases by employing a Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers with whole word masking combined with Bi-directional Long Short-Term Memory and Conditional Random Field (BERT‑wwm‑BiLSTM‑CRF) for entity recognition and BERT-wwm-BiLSTM-Attention for relation extraction. Then we retrieve a causal reasoning subgraph from this graph through relation expansion, node screening, and semantic pruning. This subgraph is provided to the large language model (LLM) to make risk assessment. Experimental results show an accuracy of 95.9%.

Christian higher education is simultaneously a confessional undertaking, an educational institution and, where it awards recognised qualifications, a subject of public academic accountability. Treating any one identity as sufficient weakens both institutional witness and learner protection. This chapter develops a biblically grounded, academically rigorous and context-sensitive account of quality governance for Christian universities, theological seminaries, ministry-training providers and faith-based programmes. A purposive critical synthesis of Scripture, historical and contemporary theological-education scholarship, curriculum and assessment theory, selected theological-education standards, and Rwandan regulatory instruments distinguishes theological commitments from empirically assessable educational claims and binding legal duties. It examines Sola Scriptura, hermeneutical competence, professional curriculum integration, doctrinal accountability, online formation, artificial intelligence, research ethics, governance, accreditation and transnational delivery. The central proposition is that mission fidelity does not substitute for educational effectiveness, and neither establishes legal recognition; instead, all three require distinct evidence and appropriate decision authority. The chapter advances a proposed Christian Higher Education Curriculum and Quality Assurance Framework situated within Integrated Evidence-Traceable Quality Governance and operationalised through a mission-alignment matrix, programme-design criteria, digital discipleship rubric, institutional self-assessment and worked hypothetical review. These instruments are neither regulator-approved nor empirically validated. The resulting approach treats faithful biblical teaching, scholarly competence, responsible stewardship and truthful public representation as mutually reinforcing obligations without confusing scriptural authority with the methods of empirical investigation or the powers of statutory regulators.

This study evaluates the diagnostic and prognostic performance of artificial intelligence in cancer detection across imaging modalities and tumor types. The review synthesizes current evidence on deep learning, radiomics, multimodal integration, and precision oncology frameworks, with emphasis on validation quality and clinical translation. A systematic review of 180 peer reviewed studies published between 2015 and 2025 was conducted. Included investigations assessed artificial intelligence applications in radiology, digital pathology, endoscopy, PET imaging, and multimodal platforms. Extracted data covered diagnostic accuracy, AUC, sensitivity, specificity, dataset size, validation strategy, and study design. Subdomains included detection, prognosis, grading, survival prediction, radio-genomics, explainability, federated learning, and regulatory evaluation. Across breast, lung, prostate, colorectal, brain, and skin cancers, multiple high-quality cohorts reported AUC values above 0.90. Whole slide histopathology achieved the highest discrimination, reaching AUC 0.99 in curated datasets. CT and MRI systems demonstrated strong performance with multicenter validation, including large scale lung and breast screening studies. Radiomics contributed to survival prediction, immunotherapy response modeling, and molecular subtype inference. Multimodal and transformer-based architectures improved representation learning in volumetric and cross domain data. Despite strong retrospective performance, only 21 percent of studies included external validation, 14 percent incorporated multicenter datasets, and 6 percent applied prospective or temporal validation. Artificial intelligence shows consistent high performance in cancer detection and prognostic modeling across imaging domains. Strongest evidence supports adjunctive use in screening, digital pathology, and endoscopic detection. Broader clinical adoption requires prospective trials, multicenter external validation, standardized reporting, explainability integration, and alignment with regulatory frameworks to ensure reliable deployment in precision oncology.

documents.abstract: Historically, General Foundation Programs (GFPs) in Oman have delivered Foundation English Language Learning (FEL) and Foundation Computing Skills (FCS) as parallel but non-communicating courses. The June 2025 revision of the Oman Core Academic Learning Outcomes (OCALOs) addresses this separation by mandating an integrated Fundamental Academic Skills (FAS) component. Unlike broader integration models such as CLIL or standalone PBL, this study synchronizes the timing of FCS instruction with the immediate requirements of FEL academic tasks, ensuring computing instruction directly serves academic output requirements. This action research study responds to that mandate by designing, piloting, and evaluating a synchronized curricular model at the School of Foundation Studies (SoFS), National University of Science and Technology (NU). Using a two-cycle action research design, the study audited existing FEL and FCS syllabi, developed a synchronized delivery plan, and piloted the model across two foundation levels totaling 79 students. Data was triangulated across student artifacts, survey responses, and faculty meeting records to evaluate skill transfer, task coherence, and student reliance on generative AI tools. The study confirmed measurable skill transfer, improved task coherence, and reduced student reliance on generative AI tools through synchronized delivery and shared assessment criteria. The key finding is that shared marking criteria between FEL and FCS faculty, rather than curriculum redesign alone, is the essential bridge that makes skill transfer successful in practice. This study offers a structural roadmap for Omani HEIs to operationalize the FAS mandate under the revised OAAAQA standards.

documents.abstract: This study examined the relationships among cognitive engagement, learning strategies, adjustment to college, academic motivation, and academic success to determine the best-fit structural equation model among Bachelor of Elementary Education students in Region XIII (Caraga), Philippines. Anchored in Self-Regulated Learning Theory and Academic Adjustment Theory, the study employed a quantitative, non-experimental descriptive-correlational design involving 470 second-, third-, and fourth-year students from three state universities, selected through proportional stratified random sampling. Data were collected using five adapted, validated, and reliability-tested questionnaires and analyzed through descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation, and structural equation modeling. Results revealed very high levels of cognitive engagement (M = 4.27), learning strategies (M = 4.32), college adjustment (M = 4.34), academic motivation (M = 4.32), and academic success (M = 4.31). All four predictors demonstrated significant positive correlations with academic success, with academic motivation exhibiting the strongest relationship (r = .519). The final structural model demonstrated excellent fit (CMIN/DF = .845, CFI = 1.000, RMSEA = .000) and explained 32.5% of the variance in academic success. Academic motivation (β = .270, p = .020) and learning strategies (β = .262, p = .017) emerged as significant direct predictors, whereas college adjustment and cognitive engagement showed nonsignificant direct effects. The findings emphasize the importance of strengthening academic motivation and effective learning strategies through learner-centered instruction and institutional support programs. The study supports Sustainable Development Goal 4 (Quality Education) by providing evidence to inform educational practices and student success initiatives. Its sustainability contribution lies in supporting evidence-based academic planning, student retention, and continuous improvement in higher education.
