documents.abstract: Abstract Field compliance checking seeks to automate the process of extracting safety requirements, capturing site information, identifying violations, and generating documentation for different responsible parties to improve construction site safety. However, existing safety checking methods are typically limited in their ability to employ domain knowledge and multimodal data, and they often lack generalizability and scalability. There is also limited effort to automatically generate natural-language descriptions of compliance-checking results for documentation purposes. Aimed toward addressing these gaps, this paper studies and compares two approaches for automated safety checking: a domain approach and an end-to-end approach. The domain approach integrates existing domain-specific information extraction, site visual information detection, and knowledge graph–based compliance reasoning methods. The end-to-end approach relies on multimodal foundation models. The comparative analysis evaluates the information extraction and compliance reasoning capabilities of both approaches in terms of performance, errors, and limitations. The results showed that the domain approach achieved strong performance with good potential for generalizability and adaptability. In contrast, the end-to-end approach requires additional fine-tuning to achieve comparable results.

This study analyses the impact of digital tools such as Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Big Data on the activities of Nigerian companies. This process is called Competitive Intelligence (CI). The study also finds that though these tools offer great opportunities, there is an “Intelligence Paradox” in Nigeria. It indicates that firms have a lot of data at hand but tend to grapple with leveraging it into proper business advice. This is largely caused by bad infrastructure like poor power supply and expensive internet, plus new privacy laws, including the Nigeria Data Protection Act (NDPA) 2023. To tackle these problems, the research recommends low-cost methods such as Open-Source Intelligence (OSINT) the use of free, public information, while ensuring humans are in charge of machines’ work. To succeed in business in Nigeria, Nigerian firms must develop their own "Compliant Intelligence" using smart technologies that are compliant with the law, the paper concludes. Mixing global technology with local knowledge helps businesses stay ahead in a tough economy.

Recent advances in computer vision, spatial computing, robotics, and embodied artificial intelligence (AI) have substantially improved machine capabilities in visual perception, navigation, spatial reasoning, and object manipulation. However, performance on structured benchmarks and controlled environments does not necessarily demonstrate equivalence to human spatial intelligence in complex real-world situations. This review examines whether current AI systems can reproduce the breadth and flexibility of human spatial and embodied intelligence, with particular emphasis on their implications for the potential replacement of humans by AI. The review synthesizes theoretical and empirical literature on human spatial cognition, embodied AI, vision-language-action models, robotics, and relevant AI capability benchmarks. The evidence is organised around four dimensions: (1) biological sensorimotor coupling and proprioception, (2) zero-shot spatial problem-solving and dynamic affordance recognition, (3) physical common-sense reasoning and adaptation, and (4) energy-efficient and context-sensitive spatial processing. Existing research indicates that AI systems have achieved considerable progress in perception, navigation, planning, and manipulation, but continue to encounter challenges involving unfamiliar environments, occlusion, uncertainty, dynamic obstacles, changing object configurations, physical interaction, long-horizon adaptation, and generalisation beyond training distributions. Human spatial intelligence, in contrast, integrates perception, proprioception, embodied experience, contextual knowledge, physical intuition, memory, and flexible real-time decision-making as an interconnected system. The reviewed evidence therefore suggests that current AI can augment and extend human spatial capabilities but cannot yet reproduce the breadth, adaptability, embodied experience, and contextual flexibility of human spatial intelligence. Spatial ability consequently represents an important dimension of human irreplaceability and supports a future paradigm of human–AI complementarity rather than complete human substitution.

As artificial intelligence (AI) moves into school education at increasing speed, we still know relatively little about how schools organise AI-related change amid policy expectations, technological uncertainty and teachers’ everyday work. Based on a qualitative case study of an AI education pilot school in Beijing, China, this article examines the formation and operation of an AI-reform professional learning community (PLC). Data were generated through semi-structured interviews, school-based observations and school documents. Through inductive thematic analysis, four recurring role functions were identified and subsequently conceptualised through the structural metaphor of the Chinese lion dance: drummers, lion heads, lion tails and audiences. The findings show that school leaders translated policy expectations and paced implementation; teacher leaders carried visible exploratory and pedagogical work; non-lead teachers extended reform through cautious and selective participation; and parents, while remaining outside the formal community, shaped ethical boundaries and conditions of trust. The article conceptualises AI-reform PLCs as issue-specific and role-differentiated communities that organise policy translation, teacher learning, leadership, participation and ethical negotiation around emerging technological change. It contributes a culturally grounded account of how school-based AI reform is collectively coordinated rather than simply implemented by individual teachers.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping agriculture by enabling data-driven decision-making across crop production systems and supporting the transition toward more sustainable, resilient, and climate-smart farming. This review critically synthesizes advances in AI applications spanning precision irrigation, nutrient and soil management, yield prediction, pest and disease monitoring, computer vision, autonomous agricultural robotics, and large language model (LLM)-based decision support systems. Beyond summarizing technological developments, the review evaluates their practical deployment, emphasizing that successful agricultural AI depends not only on predictive accuracy but also on model generalizability, explainability, economic feasibility, interoperability, and integration with existing agronomic knowledge. Emerging technologies including Vision Transformers, foundation models, Digital Twins, multimodal AI, Retrieval-Augmented Generation, and federated and continual learning—are discussed as important directions for overcoming limitations related to data scarcity, environmental variability, and scalable field implementation. The review highlights that responsible AI adoption requires transparent governance frameworks addressing data ownership, privacy, algorithmic fairness, cybersecurity, and equitable access, particularly for smallholder farming systems. Although numerous AI models report outstanding performance, widespread agricultural adoption remains constrained by cross-region validation, fragmented datasets, infrastructure requirements, and insufficient real-world deployment. Future progress will depend on multidisciplinary collaboration integrating advances in artificial intelligence, sensing technologies, robotics, crop science, and agricultural engineering to develop robust, trustworthy, and farmer-centered decision-support systems. By critically evaluating technological innovations and implementation challenges, this review provides a framework for understanding the current state of AI in agriculture while identifying research priorities that will shape the next generation of sustainable and climate-resilient agricultural systems.

This working paper is issued by the International Digital Oral History Lab (https://idohl.org/) as part of its ongoing work on the responsible use of generative AI in oral history. It brings together evidence from oral history practice, AI governance, technical infrastructure, commercial and open source platforms, professional guidance and scholarship. It examines questions of informed consent, confidentiality, shared authority, data and participant sovereignty, and the responsibilities of those who steward oral history interviews. The paper argues that data sovereignty in oral history encompasses more than storage location, privacy or legal compliance. It also concerns who controls interviews, who participates in decisions about their use, and how obligations to interviewees can be maintained within rapidly changing technological environments. This is a discussion paper rather than a definitive policy statement or a systematic review. It documents the Lab’s emerging understanding, identifies tensions and uncertainties, and contributes to discussion about responsible stewardship in an AI-mediated future. Version 1, dated 17 October 2026, was developed by the contributing authors named in the document. The International Digital Oral History Lab maintains the document and coordinates future revisions. Authorship of subsequent versions will be recorded separately.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Artificial general intelligence (AGI) has changed from a scientific aim to a moving goalpost of industrial AI ambitions. As far as the AI industry is concerned, it is simultaneously the most consequential invention in human history and a manageable, iterative technology. But what is AGI, aside from a future promise? This paper identifies four rhetorical registers through which AGI is defined, in the words of those giving it shape. In doing so, we base ourselves on the AI industry’s own discussions of AGI, including the 2026 India AI Impact Summit, AI companies’ blog posts, and journalistic coverage. Taken together, these source materials are treated as institutionalized performances of a collectively held sociotechnical imaginary through which AGI is stabilized and reproduced. As such, AGI is positioned as the next supposedly inevitable threshold on the road to superintelligence, imbued with the promise to solve all problems (a techno-solutionist register), bring prosperity (techno-utopian), pose an existential threat to humanity (techno-apocalyptic), and become no less than god (techno-theological). These rhetorical registers together capture AGI as an ineluctable sociotechnical imaginary, as it is being spoken into existence.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Aiming at the problems that the abnormal state of high-speed liquid packaging production lines is difficult to identify in time, the computing power of edge controller is limited, and the energy consumption regulation and condition monitoring are separated from each other, a multimodal lightweight artificial intelligence (AI) system embedded in Tech-Long production controller is constructed; this realizes the collaborative optimization of abnormal operation window identification and energy consumption of the whole line. First, this study collects vibration, acoustic, and thermal signals from the bottle blowing, filling, and packaging sections; it also constructs cross-sectional anomaly characterization through time synchronization, feature-level alignment, and hierarchical fusion. Subsequently, Feather Convolutional Neural Network (FeatherCNN) is reconstructed using kernel fusion, channel compression, and 4-bit Integer (INT4) quantization to reduce model computation and storage load; thus, the network can adapt to resource-constrained Advanced RISC Machine (ARM) edge controllers. Finally, a dual-layer control chain is built, composed of continuous basic energy-saving and anomaly risk-weighted correction, so that anomaly scores influence the updates of temperature zones, valve openings, and heat-sealing parameters via dynamic weights and adjustment gains. The experimental results demonstrate that the anomaly window recognition accuracy of multimodal FeatherCNN reaches 0.931, which is superior to traditional machine learning models, deep learning baselines and various single-modal structures. The lightweight processing reduces Floating-Point Operations (FLOPs) from 3.42×10⁹ to 0.58×10⁹, a decrease of approximately 83%. The inference latency of the complete model on the ARM controller is shortened from 18.63 milliseconds (ms) to 7.41 ms. Under the controlled conditions of fixed production line speed, material specifications, and statistical windows, the dual-layer collaborative control has reduced the overall energy consumption of the whole line by 26%. The results show that multimodal anomaly identification, model lightweighting, and energy-saving parameter tuning can work together in the same edge decision chain. The framework verifies the feasibility of resource-constrained controllers supporting abnormal monitoring and energy consumption regulation of the entire packaging line; meanwhile, it provides an engineering reference for edge intelligent deployment of similar high-speed liquid packaging lines.

documents.abstract: Organizations are rapidly expanding their capacity to generate and process information through data, analytics, and artificial intelligence (AI), yet greater intelligence does not necessarily translate into coordinated organizational action. As AI increasingly participates in organizational decision-making, a central managerial challenge is shifting from generating information to designing systems that transform distributed intelligence into effective decisions, coordinated action, and organizational learning. This chapter introduces Decision Supply Chain, defined as the interconnected organizational system through which signals are sensed, information is interpreted, alternatives are generated and evaluated, decisions are authorized, actions are executed, and outcomes inform subsequent decisions. The concept shifts the unit of analysis from individual decisions toward the architecture and coordination of interdependent decision activities across actors, technologies, and organizational boundaries. Although represented as a chain, the Decision Supply Chain is conceptualized as a networked and recursive system incorporating feedback, interdependence, and learning. Drawing on bounded rationality (Simon, 1957), tacit knowledge (Polanyi, 1966), Organizational Information Processing Theory (Galbraith, 1974), and research on human-AI collaboration, delegation, complementarity, and task allocation (Fügener et al., 2022, 2026; Puranam, 2021; Shrestha et al., 2019), the chapter develops a framework for Decision Supply Chain Design. It proposes that the allocation, coordination, and governance of human and AI decision activities should vary according to five characteristics of the decision context: uncertainty, consequence, reversibility, frequency, and interdependence. The framework further identifies risks arising from inappropriate human-AI configurations, including misaligned optimization, erosion of tacit knowledge, diminished human agency, and weakened organizational learning. The chapter argues that advantage from AI may depend not only on superior algorithms or information-processing capacity but increasingly on an organization's ability to orchestrate complementary human and AI capabilities across interconnected decision processes. Decision Supply Chain Design therefore offers a systems-level perspective for understanding how organizations can convert AI-enabled intelligence into coordinated action and sustained organizational learning.

documents.abstract: Welfare technologies are increasingly promoted to support people with dementia in living independently and safely. While prior research has primarily focused on user acceptance, usability, and effectiveness, less attention has been paid to the role of professionals who assess, select, and recommend these technologies. This scoping review aims to identify and map the determinants that influence prescribers’ recommendations of welfare technologies for people with dementia. The review followed an established scoping review framework and adhered to PRISMA-ScR guidelines. Searches were conducted in Scopus, Web of Science, and PubMed, focusing on empirical studies published between 2016 and 2026. Studies were included if they examined professional practices related to recommending or prescribing welfare or assistive technologies for people with dementia. Sixteen studies met the inclusion criteria and were analysed using a descriptive thematic approach. Three categories of determinants were identified: professional, organisational and systemic, and technological and contextual. Professional determinants included knowledge, experience, ethical reasoning, and assessments of user and carer capability. Organisational determinants encompassed time constraints, training, procurement systems, and availability of technologies. Technological determinants related to usability, reliability, and suitability for cognitive impairment. Across studies, recommendation emerged as a sociotechnical process shaped by the alignment between these factors. The findings highlight that access to welfare technologies is mediated by professional recommendation practices and shaped by multi-level conditions. The study contributes a fit-based understanding of recommendation, emphasising the need to address professional, organisational, and technological conditions to improve equitable access to appropriate technologies in dementia care. documents.abstract: The growth of digital assessment has intensified concerns about examination integrity, grading efficiency, fairness, and responsible artificial intelligence (AI). This study evaluates Eduvate CBT, an integrated role-based assessment ecosystem combining examination administration, AI-assisted proctoring, automated objective grading, reviewable violation evidence, and learning analytics. A four-week quantitative evaluation covered 250 undergraduate examination sessions across four computing courses, with usability data from 15 instructors and 5 administrators. At the session level, proctoring achieved 94.8% accuracy (95% CI 91.3–96.9), 94.6% precision, 96.6% recall, and an F1-score of 95.6%. Automated grading agreed with instructor consensus for 742 of 750 sampled responses (98.9%; 95% CI 97.9–99.5) and processed the cohort in under 10 s, compared with an estimated 23.1 h of manual grading. The aggregate System Usability Scale score was 87.4 (SD = 5.8; 95% CI 84.7–90.1). Analytics identified six low-performing items in algorithmic complexity, demonstrating how assessment evidence can prompt instructional review. The findings support the feasibility of the integrated workflow, although generalisability is limited by the single-institution design, absence of a competing-system control, and unavailable formal inter-rater reliability estimates.

Generative artificial intelligence (GAI) has been extensively integrated into nursing and medical education, significantly transforming the academic practices of students. Nonetheless, the varying impacts of GAI on core competency of student across educational stages remain ambiguous, with limited empirical evidence on hierarchical educational support needs. Drawing on cross-sectional comparisons of GAI-related experiences among undergraduate, master’s, and doctoral students, this study aimed to explore differences in students’ perceptions of GAI influences across educational levels. It focuses on students’ perceived impacts concerning critical thinking, research competence, and academic integrity, and further identify personalized support needs for GAI-oriented education at each stage. This cross-educational-stage comparative perspective is expected to provide empirical evidence for constructing an AI-literacy education system tailored to learners at different levels. This descriptive qualitative study draw on semi‑structured interviews with 44 students (16 undergraduate, 16 master’s, 12 doctoral) from a western Chinese medical university using inductive content analysis, with Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and AI Literacy frameworks informing discussion. Interview findings showed that GAI-use patterns varied across academic levels: undergraduates for coursework, versus postgraduates for literature reviews, experimental design, and data analysis. Students perceived that GAI-use could yield benefits for their critical thinking and knowledge acquisition, counterbalanced by risks of over-reliance, academic integrity, and cognitive offloading—with research competency gains largely confined to postgraduates. A pronounced demand for systemic support, including teacher guidance and institutional training, pervaded all levels. Interview findings suggest that GAI may exert differentiated perceived influences on the development of medical and nursing students. Students’ GAI usage patterns, academic benefits and potential risks may vary across academic levels, which suggests the necessity of adaptive educational support tailored to distinct stages. Based on qualitative findings, we propose an extended three level TAM model (PEOU driven, PU driven, critical reflection) as a preliminary conceptual framework to capture students’ different GAI use patterns. The findings may inform stratified AI literacy education and stage specific curriculum in health professions education, though further validation of this model in diverse educational contexts is still required.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GAI) can produce and revise instructional content through probabilistic, conversational interaction, creating demands that extend beyond routine use of digital tools. This study examined how digital technology knowledge and skills (DL-S) and digital application literacy (DL-A) relate to GAI-integrated technological pedagogical content knowledge (GAI-TPACK) among 224 Chinese primary and secondary teachers in general-subject settings. Participants completed a year-long professional development program and a post-intervention survey. Structural equation modeling showed positive paths from DL-S to DL-A (β = 0.300) and GAI-TPACK (β = 0.317), and from DL-A to GAI-TPACK (β = 0.453). The indirect effect of DL-S through DL-A was 0.137 (95% bootstrap CI [0.069, 0.219]), consistent with partial mediation. The larger point estimate for DL-A was not tested directly against the DL-S coefficient and is therefore interpreted descriptively. These findings position DL-A as a plausible practice-oriented mechanism linking foundational digital capability with subject-specific GAI integration. Because competence was self-reported at one post-intervention time point, the model does not establish causal development. The study offers a bounded operational account of GAI-TPACK for non-STEM professional development and identifies priorities for multi-wave and performance-based research.

Purpose: This conceptual review examines the forces driving digital disruption in the global and African insurance sectors and evaluates their implications for employment, professional competencies, and talent management, with particular attention to the role of skills-development institutions such as South Africa’s Insurance Sector Education and Training Authority (INSETA). Methodology: Drawing on Human Capital Theory and Dynamic Capabilities Theory, the study synthesizes peer-reviewed literature, industry reports, and institutional publications published predominantly between 2024 and 2026. A qualitative thematic synthesis of secondary sources was employed to identify patterns relating to technological transformation, skills shortages, evolving occupational roles, emerging risks, and institutional responses. Findings: The findings reveal that digital technologies are reshaping insurance operations and creating hybrid professional roles, yet persistent skills gaps, particularly in data analytics, artificial intelligence literacy, cybersecurity, and digital governance, constrain transformation. Regional evidence from Kenya and South Africa indicates that technological investment without corresponding human-capital development yields limited progress. Unique Contribution to Theory, Practice and Policy: The study proposes an integrated talent-intelligence framework that links technological forecasting, competency development, institutional collaboration, and continuous learning. It offers practical guidance for insurers and training providers, and informs policy on aligning education and regulation with digital insurance transformation

The development of digital transformation and Artificial Intelligence (AI) technology has brought significant changes in the world of accounting, especially in the process of recording transactions, preparing financial statements, digital audits, and fraud detection. This research aims to analyze digital transformation for accounting students in facing the development of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in the world of accounting. The research method used is Systematic Literature Review (SLR) with a thematic synthesis approach to scientific articles obtained from Google Scholar, ScienceDirect, ResearchGate, and Scopus for the 2024–2026 period. Of the 80 articles found, 15 articles that met the inclusion criteria were obtained and analyzed further. The results of the study show that digital transformation has a major impact on the accounting profession with the increasing use of accounting software, cloud computing, blockchain, and AI in business processes. Accounting students are required not only to understand accounting theory, but also to have digital competencies such as mastery of accounting information systems, data analysis, and the use of AI-based technology. Factors that affect students' readiness to face AI include digital literacy, educational curriculum, technology access, and adaptability. In addition to presenting challenges in the form of increasing job competition and the need for technology skills, AI also opens up new opportunities in the accounting profession such as digital auditors, financial data analysts, and information systems consultants. Therefore, universities need to update the curriculum to be more relevant to technological developments and industrial needs in the digital era.

Contractor safety management in large-scale industries—particularly within the process and heavy industrial sectors—faces chronic structural challenges: information fragmentation across siloed, paper-based systems; the manual verification of document validity; and, consequently, a reactive approach to qualification processes. To address these gaps, this research proposes and justifies a system termed the "Smart Contractor Passport." By establishing a unified digital profile for every contractor and individual working under a contract, this system consolidates identity data, contractual details, training records, occupational health examination results, and site-access authorization status into a single source of truth.The research employs a documentary-analytical approach. First, it analyzes domestic legal requirements—specifically Articles 13, 85, and 91 of the Labor Law, along with the 2010 Safety Regulations for Contracting Operations—as well as the ISO 45001:2018 standard. Subsequently, it identifies process gaps in the current state and translates them into functional system requirements. The proposed architecture rests on three pillars: the digitization of records; the integration of processes across the HSE, security, contracts, training, and occupational health departments; and conditional access control utilizing QR code and NFC tokens. The results of a comparative analysis indicate that transitioning from a reactive model to a proactive, data-driven one—by eliminating human error in qualification verification and preventing the entry of unqualified individuals or those with expired credentials—mitigates legal and financial risks for the employer, while establishing an infrastructure for auditing and real-time decision-making.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: With the rapid advancement of artificial intelligence technologies, AI-driven medical image classification has attracted considerable attention in recent years. However, increasingly stringent data privacy regulations have significantly restricted data sharing among medical institutions, making it difficult for traditional centralized learning frameworks to effectively exploit distributed medical data resources. As a privacy-preserving distributed machine learning paradigm, federated learning enables multiple institutions to collaboratively train models without directly exchanging raw data. Nevertheless, federated learning still faces several critical challenges in practical applications, including heterogeneous data distributions and model bias caused by non-independent and identically distributed (Non-IID) data. To address these challenges, this paper proposes a dynamic weighted learning method based on federated contrastive learning. Different from approaches that focus solely on local representation optimization or employ fixed aggregation weights, the proposed framework couples supervised contrastive local training with loss-feedback-based multi-factor client weighting, thereby jointly controlling local representation drift and server-side model aggregation. Specifically, contrastive learning is integrated into the federated learning framework by jointly leveraging local and global model representations for supervised contrastive optimization. This strategy effectively mitigates the distribution discrepancy among different clients and gradually aligns local models with the global model as communication rounds progress. Furthermore, during global aggregation, a loss-feedback rule is introduced to accept the candidate global model parameters and aggregation weights only when the candidate loss-feedback value decreases. In addition, a multi-factor weighted aggregation mechanism is introduced to comprehensively evaluate client contributions based on multiple factors, thereby assigning larger aggregation weights to local models that are more beneficial to global model optimization. Experiments were conducted on an osteoporosis knee X-ray dataset and a COVID–Pneumonia–Normal chest X-ray dataset under IID and different Non-IID settings. Under severe Non-IID conditions, the proposed method achieved accuracies of 92.12% and 96.27%, area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) values of 98.31% and 97.68%, and F1 scores of 90.92% and 93.22% on the two datasets, respectively. Comparisons with representative federated learning methods and the static-weighting ablation setting demonstrate that the proposed method maintains competitive classification performance and stable training behavior under heterogeneous client distributions.

documents.abstract: During the 1970s, as computerization became central to Japan’s public administration, the state advanced a sociotechnical imaginary of an efficient, digitally unified information society, built on integrating personal data and culminating in a proposed national identification number. In response, a social movement emerged to contest the concentration of informational power in state and corporate systems. This article argues that the movement is best understood as a politics of anticipation. It mobilized against a data state that did not yet exist, contesting the imaginary as a claim about the future, not present harms. Drawing on imported and projected examples, activists fought on two fronts, protection of personal data and access to government information, in an anticipatory contest that co-produced Japan’s data-governance regime. Tracing the movement from the 1972 founding of the Central Council for Opposing the National ID System and Protecting Privacy through census resistance and activists’ entry into local government, the article shows that the feared data state arrived only in constrained form, hedged by the oversight the movement had demanded. Neither the imaginary’s triumph nor the movement’s victory, the resulting settlement turns on the question it first raised: who should control the collection, circulation, and use of personal information?

Abstract Non-compliance with Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) use regulations, particularly helmet wearing, remains a critical occupational safety challenge in high-risk industrial environments. This study investigates how hierarchical prompt engineering shapes the quality of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) generated by Large Language Models (LLMs) for image-level helmet-wearing compliance classification (helmet vs. no-helmet) as a mechanism for PPE compliance monitoring. Four LLMs (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and Grok) produced executable PyTorch scripts across three prompt tiers of increasing specificity. These configurations were evaluated over 20 independent runs on a purpose-built dataset of 972 balanced images, using six classification metrics, four prompt quality metrics, and three resource efficiency dimensions. Ten of the twelve configurations converged to a high-performance plateau (accuracy 0.957-−0.967, AUC 0.985-−0.993). Claude at Tier 1 achieved the highest accuracy (0.967) and the lowest CPU usage (12.2%), whereas the best-calibrated (lowest-loss) pipelines were produced by Gemini and Grok at Tier 1 (test loss 0.127 and 0.142), reflecting an accuracy–calibration dissociation that we analyze in detail. However, Gemini and Grok experienced catastrophic convergence failures at Tier 3 (accuracy $$\approx $$ 0.58), revealing that over-specification of architectural and training constraints can destabilize CNN generation even when the produced scripts are syntactically valid. Higher prompt specificity does not consistently improve accuracy or validity rate. Instead, LLM identity interacts strongly with the prompt tier and emerges as a more critical factor than prompt design alone, although each LLM–tier condition is represented by a single generated script. Within the scope of this controlled, image-level evaluation, basic and structured prompting represent the recommended operating range for developing PPE compliance classifiers, delivering competitive accuracy and full validity rate across all models without the convergence failures observed at Tier 3. Validation in real industrial settings remains necessary.

Low back injuries are common among commercial fishermen and have been linked to physically demanding tasks involved in fishing operations. Occupational back-support exoskeletons (BSEs) may help reduce low back physical demands, but their effectiveness in commercial fishing has not been well studied. This study evaluated the effects of two passive BSEs on muscle activity and joint kinematics in 20 male participants performing simulated crab sorting and pot handling tasks with and without two rigid BSEs. Results showed that both BSEs significantly reduced erector spinae muscle activity, with larger reductions during crab sorting than during pot handling. BSE use also led to some unintended changes in abdominal and leg muscle activity and joint kinematics, depending on the task and device used. These findings suggest that BSEs may help reduce low back demands during commercial crabbing, while highlighting the need to further evaluate potential side effects, especially during long-term use under real-world fishing conditions.

This pilot study investigated distance estimation, subjective fear, and lower-extremity muscle activity during physically embodied ladder climbing in immersive virtual reality (VR). Ten participants climbed an 8-foot ladder registered to a virtual ladder and were exposed to eight simulated elevations ranging from 0 to 100 m across two sessions. At each elevation, participants rated their fear, estimated distances to the ground and an overhead target, and completed a brief ascent and descent while muscle activity was recorded. Linear mixed-effects models showed that actual distance significantly predicted estimation error, with increasingly negative error as elevation increased, indicating greater underestimation at larger distances. Viewing direction had no significant effect. Fear increased significantly with virtual height and was lower during the second exposure session. Lower-extremity muscle activity did not differ significantly across height conditions. These findings show that ladder climbing in VR can elicit height-dependent changes in perceptual judgments and fear. The study demonstrates a method for increasing interaction fidelity in VR research on height perception and supports further investigation with larger samples and refined physiological measures.

Abstract and Research Description This research is the third installment of Egypt’s Comprehensive Development Vision, a broader initiative exploring strategic approaches to Egypt’s long-term development and national transformation. The study presents a comprehensive conceptual framework for developing state institutions, strengthening strategic planning, improving public administration, advancing education and human capital, promoting technological innovation and artificial intelligence, and enhancing accountability and institutional effectiveness. It explores the metaphor of the state as a living organism, examining the interconnected roles of national leadership, citizens, intelligence and strategic analysis, defense institutions, legislative bodies, public oversight, and essential infrastructure. The research also proposes approaches to urban and regional development, the modernization of Egyptian cities and villages, the development of religious and educational institutions, the intellectual advancement of society, the growth of domestic technology and digital platforms, and the sustainable use of national resources, including the Nile River and its islands. In addition to presenting strategic proposals, the study explores practical implementation mechanisms, institutional coordination, performance measurement, innovation initiatives, and long-term planning. Its objective is to develop an integrated vision that connects human development, institutional reform, scientific progress, technological capability, economic advancement, cultural identity, and national sustainability. This document is published in both English and Arabic. The complete English version appears first, followed by the complete original Arabic version, making the research accessible to international readers as well as Arabic-speaking audiences. This work forms part of an ongoing conceptual research series dedicated to exploring ideas and proposals for Egypt’s future development. The proposals are intended to encourage strategic thinking, constructive discussion, and the development of practical solutions suited to Egypt’s national priorities and circumstances.

Arthritis is one of the leading causes of chronic pain, disability, and reduced quality of life worldwide, affecting millions of individuals through progressive joint inflammation, cartilage degeneration, and bone destruction. Although conventional therapies, including nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), glucocorticoids, disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs), biologics, and Janus kinase (JAK) inhibitors, effectively alleviate symptoms and delay disease progression, their long-term use is frequently associated with adverse effects, high treatment costs, and incomplete disease remission. Consequently, phytotherapy has emerged as a promising complementary and alternative therapeutic strategy owing to its multitarget pharmacological actions and comparatively favorable safety profile. This review comprehensively summarizes the current knowledge on the pathophysiology of arthritis, emphasizing inflammatory cytokines, oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and major intracellular signaling pathways, including NF-κB, MAPK, JAK/STAT, PI3K/Akt, NLRP3 inflammasome, COX-2, and 5-lipoxygenase. Particular attention is given to bioactive phytoconstituents such as curcumin, resveratrol, quercetin, kaempferol, luteolin, apigenin, catechins, boswellic acids, thymoquinone, berberine, and other polyphenols, flavonoids, terpenoids, alkaloids, saponins, tannins, and glycosides. Furthermore, the review compiles experimental pharmacological evidence from in vitro and in vivo studies, summarizes medicinal plants with established anti-arthritic activity, and highlights their molecular targets and mechanisms of action. Emerging advances in nanotechnology-based phytopharmaceuticals, molecular docking, network pharmacology, omics technologies, and artificial intelligence are also discussed as future directions for improving the efficacy, bioavailability, and precision of plant-derived therapeutics. Collectively, the available evidence indicates that phytochemicals exert anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, immunomodulatory, and chondroprotective effects through simultaneous modulation of multiple molecular pathways. However, further standardization, pharmacokinetic evaluation, and well-designed multicenter clinical trials are required to facilitate their successful translation into evidence-based clinical practice. This review provides an integrated scientific framework for researchers and clinicians involved in the development of safer, multitarget, and effective phytotherapeutic interventions for arthritis management.

This study emphasizes the role of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in aiding Omani students in the General Foundation Program to learn English as a Foreign Language (EFL). Despite the growing use of AI tools like ChatGPT, Google Translate, and Grammarly, there is limited research in Oman on learners' attitudes and the implications of AI for vocabulary instruction. A mixed-methods research design was used, and the sample comprised 151 respondents studying in the Sultanate of Oman. SPSS version 29 was used to analyze the quantitative data. The qualitative data revealed that EFL Omani students relied heavily on ChatGPT (49.7%) as the most widely used AI tool, followed by Google Translate (21.2%), Gemini AI (17.9%), Grammarly (6.6%). In addition, the trust in AI (frequency: 60), followed by cross-checking the meaning with other reliable resources (frequency: 67), learner autonomy (frequency: 67), and academic honesty (frequency: 64), but learning grammar, enhancing writing and reading skills had the lowest frequency. The quantitative data indicate an overall mean score of 3.67, suggesting a high frequency of AI tool use for vocabulary learning. The lowest mean score, 3.45, corresponds to the students' trust in the new vocabulary suggested by AI tools. In contrast, the effectiveness of AI tools received the highest mean score of 3.92. Additionally, it was found that AI tools, learners' attitudes and challenges, learning strategies, digital literacy, and how factors such as gender and academic level affect AI-assisted vocabulary learning in EFL Omani students were examined for vocabulary acquisition.

Patients who participate in intracranial neuroscience research make invaluable contributions to our understanding of the brain, accelerating the development of neurotechnological interventions. Engagement of patients as part of this research presents unique challenges, where study goals can be distant from immediate clinical applications and require specialized domain knowledge. Yet methods for meaningfully integrating patient communities as part of these research efforts are essential, as intracranial neuroscience guides the application of artificial intelligence (AI) for understanding and enhancing human cognition. In order to identify what patients consider meaningful research engagement we interviewed individuals who participated in a study during their Deep Brain Stimulation (DBS) surgery and attended a group event where they interacted with our research team. Analysis of semi-structured interviews identified four main themes: interest in science and the future of clinical care, contributing to science to improve lives, connecting with others, and accessibility considerations. Based on these insights, we propose strategies for transformational participation of patient communities in intracranial neuroscience research with respect to engagement objectives, communication and scope. This approach offers a foundation for sustaining relationships between scientists and communities rooted in trust and transparency, to ensure that impacts of AI-driven neurotechnology on human health and cognition are aligned with patient needs as well as desired public values.

As Advanced Driver Assistance Systems (ADAS) become increasingly common in modern vehicles, drivers often misunderstand how these systems work and when they reach their limits, which can lead to unsafe driving behaviors. This study examined how training modes (video vs. in-vehicle) and training styles (demonstration vs. practice) affect drivers’ ADAS knowledge improvement and decision-making accuracy when responding to system limitations. Sixty participants were assigned to one of four conditions covering three Level 1 and Level 2 ADAS features: Adaptive Cruise Control, Lane Keeping Assist, and Partial Automation. In-vehicle training produced greater knowledge gains than video-based training overall. For Partial Automation specifically, in-vehicle demonstration and video-based practice both outperformed video demonstration. However, knowledge improvement did not translate to better decision-making accuracy in any condition. These findings suggest that ADAS training should go beyond teaching system limitations and also help drivers apply that knowledge when system limitations occur during driving.

Entrepreneurial performance is a multidimensional phenomenon that is influenced by the psychological attributes, individual competencies, organisational capabilities, financial resources, technological developments and environment. This is crucial for fostering entrepreneurship effectiveness and sustainable entrepreneurship development as these determinants are interrelated. The key factors affecting the performance of entrepreneurs are explored, focusing on emotional intelligence, entrepreneurial orientation, education, the digital transformation, financial capabilities, institutional support and sustainability. The review brings together literature on psychological and individual factors, entrepreneurial orientation and competency building, digital transformation and financial skills, as well as environmental, institutional and sustainable entrepreneurship. The reviewed studies have identified emotional intelligence as a salient psychological factor that facilitates emotional control, making decisions, coping with adversity, interpersonal relationships, leadership, and flexibility in the face of unpredictable business environments. The other factors that contribute to opportunity recognition, innovation, entrepreneurial intention, and venture development are entrepreneurial education, experiential learning, digital competencies and entrepreneurial orientation. Digital technologies and artificial intelligence, cloud computing, digital platforms and other technologies offer opportunities to enhance resource mobilisation, market access and organisational performance, but face issues of digital inequality, ethical governance and technological capacity. Entrepreneurial development and the ability to embrace sustainable business practices are also affected by financial literacy, access to finance, saving patterns and green finance.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming entrepreneurship by enhancing innovation, decision-making, and operational efficiency. However, unequal access to technology, limited digital literacy, and ethical concerns constrain inclusive AI adoption, particularly among underserved entrepreneurial communities. This study systematically reviews how entrepreneurship education promotes inclusive AI adoption and supports sustainable business growth. Guided by the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) framework, the study examined literature published between 2015 and 2025 across five databases: Scopus, Web of Science, Google Scholar, ScienceDirect, and SpringerLink. Following screening and eligibility assessment, 54 studies were included. Findings indicate that AI literacy, adaptive learning platforms, digital mentorship, and practical business simulations can strengthen entrepreneurial competencies, innovation, and data-driven decision-making. Inclusive AI adoption is also associated with improved operational efficiency, competitiveness, and resource utilization. However, barriers include inadequate digital infrastructure, high implementation costs, algorithmic bias, and data privacy concerns. The review highlights limited evidence on long-term outcomes and environmental sustainability. Drawing on Human Capital Theory, the Technology Acceptance Model, and Innovation Diffusion Theory, the study contributes an integrated perspective on inclusive AI, entrepreneurship education, and sustainability. It recommends inclusive curricula, ethical AI governance, accessible infrastructure, and targeted policy support to promote equitable and sustainable entrepreneurial growth.

Abstract: Cyberbiosecurity increasingly depends on digital systems to observe, represent, interpret and control biological processes. This dependence creates a class of threats whose principal effect may not be destruction, denial, or conventional evasion, but degradation of the defender's ability to recognize the biological or security state being observed. This paper introduces a technical framework for practical cyber epistemic pathogens: biological, technical or sociotechnical threat processes whose security-relevant indicators are systematically suppressed, distorted, misclassified, fragmented, forgotten, normalized or prevented from converging into actionable knowledge as they pass through sensing, analysis, organizational memory and response systems. We use the term “antimemetic” to describe the knowledge-evasive effects of such threats while distinguishing these effects from conventional stealth, deception, anti-forensics, and data-integrity attacks. A conceptual taxonomy is developed through a purposive structured synthesis of cyberbiosecurity and adjacent literature, informed by established taxonomy-development methodology. The framework organizes cyber-biological knowledge formation as an epistemic pathogenesis pathway from biological ground truth through observation, digital representation, interpretation, contextual correlation, knowledge formation, organizational memory, and action. Seven mechanisms are identified: observational suppression, representational distortion, semantic camouflage, contextual fragmentation, mnemonic erosion, normalization, and consensus disruption. These mechanisms are embedded within a multidimensional taxonomy describing origin, intentionality, persistence, propagation, primary knowledgestate effect, and consequence domain. The paper further introduces epistemic fidelity as the degree to which a human-machine defensive system maintains a decision-relevant correspondence with cyber-biological ground truth. Application across genomic databases, nucleic-acid screening, biomanufacturing, laboratory systems and autonomous laboratories show how heterogeneous vulnerabilities can produce structurally similar failures of defensive knowledge. Finally, the paper develops the prospective concept of epistemic lock-in, in which erroneous observations influence automated biological actions that generate subsequent evidence reinforcing the original false model. The framework reframes cyberbiosecurity from protecting biological and digital assets alone towards protecting the processes through which those assets become reliably knowable. By treating knowledge formation as a security surface, the taxonomy offers a common language for comparing otherwise dissimilar cyber-biological failures and for designing future assessment, red-teaming, and resilience measures.

Background: Educational technology and artificial intelligence (AI) are transforming nursing education by expanding approaches to instruction, assessment, and clinical simulation. These innovations offer opportunities to enhance learning while creating ethical, professional, and pedagogical challenges requiring thoughtful evaluation. Purpose: This paper examines the ethical implications of integrating AI and educational technology into nursing education and explores strategies for implementation that preserve professional standards, equity, academic integrity, and educational quality. Discussion: AI integration in nursing education raises concerns related to privacy, accessibility, digital competence, academic integrity, and the student-faculty relationship. Increased reliance on digital platforms requires strong data governance and compliance with regulations such as the Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act (FERPA) to protect student information. Limited access to technology may also contribute to educational inequities. Faculty and student development are essential to promote responsible technology use. Generative AI introduces concerns regarding plagiarism, misinformation, and potential effects on critical thinking and clinical reasoning. Nursing programs must establish clear guidelines for ethical AI use while ensuring that technology complements rather than replaces faculty mentorship and human connection. Ethical Analysis: Ethical technology integration should reflect nursing values of caring, compassion, justice, respect, and accountability. AI can support learning, feedback, and clinical reasoning but should not replace professional judgment or moral responsibility. The American Nurses Association emphasizes that AI should augment nursing practice while maintaining professional accountability (ANA, 2015). AI-generated information should inform, not determine, high-stakes academic decisions, with transparency, human oversight, and opportunities for review. Implications and Conclusion: Ethical adoption of AI prepares future nurses for digital healthcare environments by strengthening technological literacy, ethical reasoning, and equitable access to learning. Nurse educators play a critical role in modeling responsible technology use. Successful integration requires faculty development, institutional support, and ethical frameworks that balance innovation with accountability while preserving nursing’s commitment to compassionate, evidence-based care.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming dermatology at a rapid pace unlike any other clinical specialty, largely because skin disease is diagnosed visually and, therefore, lends itself naturally to image-based machine learning. Convolutional neural networks now correspond with dermatologists in classifying pigmented lesions, teledermatology platforms triage patients across vast distances, and AI-enabled applications are increasingly available on patients’ screens. Yet this rapid uptake has outpaced the ethical and regulatory scaffolding needed to govern it safely. The Indian Council of Medical Research has addressed this gap conscientiously in March 2023 by publishing the Ethical Guidelines for Application of AI in Biomedical Research and Healthcare, India’s first dedicated ethics framework for medical AI. This article examines the ethical dimensions of AI in dermatology research and clinical practice through the lens of these guidelines, drawing on dermatology-specific evidence on algorithmic bias, consent, data privacy, transparency, and accountability, with recommendations for dermatologists, researchers, and ethics committees engaging with this technology.

documents.abstract: Traffic safety countermeasure recommendation requires simultaneous consideration of crash context, roadway facility, traffic control, operating conditions, and evidence applicability. Traditional rule-based and keyword-matching methods have difficulty processing natural-language crash-context queries. This study proposes an evidence-grounded and mechanism-aware framework that formulates traffic safety countermeasure recommendation as the construction, selection, and ranking of CMF Evidence Cards. A structured CMF Evidence Store containing 8844 Evidence Cards was developed from the CMF Clearinghouse. A corpus of 2935 crash-context queries was further constructed, including 1935 complete queries and 1000 controlled incomplete variants. For each query, the framework constructs a candidate evidence pool through Context-aware Retrieval, Mechanism-aware Recall Augmentation, and Engineering Applicability Filtering. A large language model fine-tuned through supervised learning then selects and ranks up to three Evidence IDs and returns the corresponding countermeasure descriptions, CMF or CRF values, evidence quality, applicability conditions, and literature sources. The fine-tuned Qwen3-32B achieved an Exact Evidence Top-1 of 53.14%, an Exact Evidence Hit@3 of 76.15%, a Mechanism Hit@3 of 83.26%, an Exact Evidence Jaccard of 44.18%, and an Empty-set Decision Accuracy of 95.08%. Module-level ablation results confirmed the distinct contributions of the three candidate evidence construction components. Candidate-pool sensitivity analysis showed that evidence coverage reached saturation at approximately 30 Evidence Cards. The proposed framework also substantially outperformed a conventional BM25-RAG baseline and maintained stable performance across semantically equivalent query paraphrases. LLM-assisted and independent expert evaluations further supported the contextual relevance, mechanism consistency, engineering applicability, and overall usefulness of the recommendations. Case studies demonstrated the framework's ability to address mechanism-complex and facility-specific traffic safety scenarios, while also identifying evidence retrieval as a limitation in specialized contexts such as work zones.
topics: IoT and GPS-based Vehicle Safety Systems

documents.abstract: To promote the design of low-carbon alkali-activated materials, precise yet interpretable compressive strength prediction based on mix design variables is essential to minimize trial-and-error experimentation. This study employs an interpretable machine learning approach to predict compressive strength based on important mix design variables, including fly ash content, ground granulated blast furnace slag content, Na 2 O content, SiO 2 /Na 2 O ratio and water to binder ratio. Various ensemble machine learning models, such as Random Forest, Gradient Boosting Decision Tree, XGBoost, and LightGBM were developed and compared for model performance evaluation using R 2 , RMSE and MAE. Among the models, the Random Forest model had the best generalization performance with a test coefficient R² of 0.762, along with RMSE of 9.23 MPa and MAE of 6.38 MPa. Explainable artificial intelligence techniques were then used to interpret the machine learning model predictions and determine the variable contributions. The results consistently showed that the water to binder ratio is the most dominant factor influencing the compressive strength, followed by Na 2 O content, fly ash content and SiO 2 /Na 2 O ratio. A clear nonlinear threshold was found at a water to binder ratio of approximately 0.5, beyond which the predicted compressive strength dropped rapidly. Therefore, the interpretable machine learning framework presented in this study minimizes trial-and-error experimentation by providing accurate compressive strength prediction and clear, mix-design-related explanations for the development of low-carbon alkali-activated materials.

Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is transforming the possibilities for informal language learning by providing immediate feedback, conversational interaction, and potentially personalized learning experiences. However, its use does not necessarily entail greater learner autonomy, self-regulation, or agency. This study aimed to understand how Colombian adults configure their informal English learning practices through GenAI tools, with particular attention to decision-making processes, self-regulation, evaluation of AI-generated responses, and the articulation of GenAI with other learning resources. Adopting a qualitative, exploratory, and interpretive approach, the study involved four Colombian adults with diverse linguistic, educational, and GenAI-use trajectories. Data were generated through participant characterization forms, GenAI interaction records, semi-structured interviews, and, when available, documentary evidence of participants’ interactions with the technology. A predominantly inductive thematic analysis generated four interconnected categories: negotiating control over the learning interaction; constructing and calibrating trust in AI-generated feedback; experiencing personalization through responsive interaction; and reconfiguring the broader learning repertoire. Findings show that participants assumed, negotiated, and delegated control in different ways and developed varying criteria for accepting, questioning, or verifying GenAI-generated responses. They also selectively integrated GenAI with other digital and human learning resources. Based on these findings, the study conceptualizes GenAI appropriation as a form of situated orchestration through which learners coordinate technological affordances with their purposes, prior knowledge, evaluative criteria, and broader learning repertoires. The findings suggest that GenAI does not automatically produce learner autonomy or agency; rather, it creates new spaces in which these may be exercised, negotiated, or delegated.

The rapid integration of large language models (LLMs) into multilingual digital environments has raised specific questions about contextual appropriateness, sociopragmatic calibration, and interactional adaptation across culturally situated norms. While benchmarks have evaluated LLM performance across dozens of languages, these assessments remain confined to classification tasks and are not designed to assess productive sociopragmatic competence in underrepresented ecologies such as Indonesian. This study compares speech act production between three flagship LLMs (GPT-5, Claude Opus 4.1, Gemini 3 Pro) and 150 Indonesian native speakers. Data were elicited using a 16-scenario Discourse Completion Task spanning requests, refusals, complaints, and apologies across varied power (+/-P) and distance (+/-D) configurations. Responses were coded using an adapted Cross-Cultural Speech Act Realization Patterns (CCSARP) framework and digital-pragmatic categories capturing emoji, phatic markers, colloquial particles, and code-mixing characteristic of Indonesian online discourse. Results indicate that while all three LLMs produced grammatically well-formed and strategically recognisable speech acts, significant divergences emerged in face-work calibration, scalar modification, and text-based digital-pragmatic signalling. All models systematically preferred negative politeness strategies and used basa-basi (phatic communion), colloquial particles, code-mixing, and emoji less frequently, while deploying honorifics with less contextual specificity than human responses. Claude Opus 4.1 exhibited the most conservative profile, while Gemini 3 Pro showed the greatest contextual sensitivity, though all remained distinct from the Indonesian native-speaker comparison group. These findings provide an early production-based empirical comparison of LLM pragmatic alignment in Indonesian digital interaction, contributing to computational sociopragmatics with implications for AI safety, cross-cultural NLP evaluation, and sociopragmatically aware language technologies.

Introduction: Low back pain (LBP) is an important occupational health concern among dental students and practising dentists. This systematic review aimed to synthesise evidence on ergonomic and individual factors associated with LBP, distinguish directly measured findings from hypothesised biomechanical or anatomical pathways, and identify implications for multilevel occupational health promotion. Methods: This systematic review followed the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidance. PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science Core Collection, and Google Scholar were searched for English-language studies published from 1 January 2021 through 31 May 2026. Two reviewers independently screened records and extracted data. Of 327 records identified, 24 full-text reports were assessed and 6 studies were included in a qualitative synthesis because populations, exposures, outcomes, and analytical methods were heterogeneous. Results: Six studies were included. The studies directly assessed self-reported LBP or disability, working posture, sitting duration, physical activity, age, body mass index, years of practice, and, in one study, trunk-movement parameters. Estimates from students and practising dentists were not directly comparable. Non-neutral posture and selected occupational or individual factors were associated with LBP in some studies, but findings were inconsistent for sitting duration, physical activity, and years of practice. Proposed changes in lumbar loading, alignment, or stability were not directly measured in most studies. Conclusion: Available evidence suggests associations between selected ergonomic or individual factors and LBP among dental students and practising dentists, but heterogeneous populations, predominantly cross-sectional designs, and self-reported measures limit causal inference. The findings may inform candidate occupational health-promotion actions at the individual, professional-education, work-organisation, and clinical-environment levels; however, the included studies did not evaluate their effectiveness. Prospective controlled studies are required before preventive effectiveness can be inferred.

This systematic literature review analyses factors associated with research literacy among university students based on 50 studies published between 1 January 2015 and 31 December 2025. Following PRISMA guidelines, studies were selected from Scopus, Web of Science, and Science Direct databases. The findings reveal research literacy as a multidimensional competency operating through three interconnected dimensions — personal (63%), pedagogical (23%) and institutional (14%), computed over the 35 studies with extractable quantitative data —. Personal factors showed the strongest statistical associations, with information literacy (d = 0.82) and research self-efficacy (d = 0.76) yielding the largest pooled effect sizes. Pedagogical factors, though less represented, were associated with the largest effect sizes, particularly library-faculty collaboration (d = 0.94) and structured instruction (d = 0.78). Institutional factors, including frameworks and technological resources, were consistently associated with larger estimates for personal and pedagogical variables, a pattern compatible with — but not demonstrative of — an amplifying role. The review identified a paradigmatic shift from traditional information literacy toward critical artificial intelligence literacy, with a 410% growth in AI-related studies between 2023–2025. Bibliometric analysis revealed geographical concentration in Europe and Asia (50%), highlighting underrepresentation of Global South perspectives. Methodological limitations include predominance of correlational designs (36%) and scarcity of longitudinal studies (12%). The study proposes an explanatory framework in which institutional conditions operate as contextual antecedents that shape instructional opportunity, which in turn relates to individual research competence through research self-efficacy, with discipline, academic stage and prior digital competence acting as moderators; four testable propositions are derived from it. Because the evidence base is predominantly correlational, these findings should be read as associations rather than causal effects; they provide an evidence-informed basis for designing educational strategies intended to foster critical thinking, information evaluation, and ethical research practices in contemporary higher education contexts.

Repeated users of an artificial-intelligence agent may learn both its competence and how it sounds. This paper proposes that acquired style congruence can change acceptance independently of evidential quality, while any benefit to error management may arise through more than one route. Learned style–correctness contingencies can guide classification; reduced processing demands may also free attention for substantive checking when style itself is non-diagnostic. The framework distinguishes recognition, response criterion, classification sensitivity, competence learning, defect identification, successful correction, and final accuracy. Five competing mechanisms are specified: familiarity halo, anomaly vigilance, diagnostic cue learning, competence learning, and processing-efficiency learning. Building on appropriate-reliance research, calibration symmetry is treated as a requirement for identification and measurement: both familiar-looking wrong answers and unfamiliar-looking correct answers must be examined. It does not imply equal frequency, cost, or normative importance. The contribution is a bounded synthesis for acquired, source-specific style, not a new general principle of reliance or a demonstrated familiarity effect. Study 1 crosses acquired style congruence with correctness while preserving randomized assignment and measuring inferred source or version change. Study 2 varies cue diagnosticity and distinguishes classification through style from identifying and repairing substantive defects. Outcome feedback, trial-level learning, delayed unaided performance, and transfer are specified separately from assisted performance. Conversational affirmation and linguistic accommodation are adjacent pathways, not evidence of acquired-style effects. Governance implications remain provisional pending direct evidence.

The Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT) has become a fundamental component of modern industrial automation by connecting sensors, actuators, programmable logic controllers, robotic systems, machines, edge devices, and cloud platforms for continuous monitoring and intelligent control. However, the dependence of industrial operations on interconnected IoT networks introduces significant risks associated with communication failures, sensor faults, hardware degradation, software errors, cyber-attacks, congestion, and edge computing failures. A single failure can interrupt production, reduce product quality, increase maintenance costs, or create safety hazards. This paper examines the application of Artificial Intelligence (AI) to improve fault tolerance in IoT networks used for industrial automation. The paper reviews recent developments in AI based fault detection, anomaly detection, predictive maintenance, intelligent routing, and edge based recovery, and adaptive resource management. Recent studies demonstrate that machine learning can identify abnormal device and sensor behavior before failures propagate, while Software Defined Networking can support rapid route restoration and network recovery. AI enabled edge computing further reduces response latency by moving fault analysis closer to industrial devices. The paper proposes a conceptual AI enabled fault tolerant architecture consisting of an IoT sensing layer, resilient communication layer, edge intelligence layer, AI fault analysis layer, decision and recovery layer, and industrial control layer. The proposed approach combines real-time monitoring, machine-learning-based prediction, redundant communication paths, automated recovery, and predictive maintenance. The paper concludes that integrating AI with fault-tolerance mechanisms can improve industrial network availability, reliability, resilience, and operational continuity. Nevertheless, challenges involving data quality, explain ability, computational resources, cyber security, interoperability, and validation in real industrial environments require further investigation.

documents.abstract: Whether students develop dependency on generative artificial intelligence (AI) technologies largely depends on their attitudes toward using such tools. Existing studies have primarily explained the formation of AI dependency from the perspectives of usage attitude and technological characteristics, while paying limited attention to the psychological mechanisms through which attitudes exert their influence. Grounded in Self-Determination Theory, the present study examines how different types of use motivation mediate the relationship between students’ AI attitude and AI dependency. A total of 405 university students completed a comprehensive questionnaire measuring AI attitude, use motivations, and AI dependency. The results indicate that: (i) AI attitude does not directly predict AI dependency; instead, its effects are transmitted through multiple motivational pathways, with intrinsic motivation inhibiting AI dependency, whereas identified regulation facilitates its development; (ii) three distinct AI dependency profiles were identified: dependent, moderate, and conservative users. These profiles exhibited clear stratification, with dependent users showing the highest scores across all dimensions and conservative users the lowest; and (iii) individuals with stronger motivations are more likely to be classified into the dependent user profile, with external motivation playing a particularly salient role. These findings enrich the literature on AI dependency and offer practical implications for higher education administrators, tool developers, and educational researchers.

Rapid progress in digital media and artificial intelligence is transforming human communication, facilitating the rapid exchange of messages and minimizing the chances of reflective interpretation. Existing theories in linguistics, psychology, and cultural studies address the structural, cognitive, or social aspects of language, yet fail to explain how emotional processing, internal linguistic structuring, and culturally mediated communication function as a coherent, dynamic system. Through this model, the authors present the AL–DL–CL framework that explores how three layers are engaged in a process that results in communication, through a recursive interaction between the Automatic Layer (AL), the Deliberate Layer (DL), and the Cultural Language Layer (CL). In such a process, the affective or unconscious processes in AL are consistently reframed into structured internal representations via DL, and through CL, and translated back into culturally-expressed language serves as a feedback mechanism, with a tendency to modify cognition and emotional response. Based on a multi-method exploratory approach of sequential cultural transmission, clinical case study analysis, and group-based validation, the results indicate that language is not so much a static container for meaning as a process of reconstruction that is molded by the dynamic interaction between emotion, cognition, and culture. This model also demonstrates how digitally mediated communication can amplify AL-directed reaction and limit DL-level thinking, which increases the potential for misinterpretation, polarization, or misinformation. The AL–DL–CL framework provides guidance in a unified theoretical perspective around language emergence, responsible AI design and digital literacy and intercultural discourse based on the continuous transformation system of communication, and not on the linear encoding.

Generative AI functions as an information service in which prompting can simultaneously seek information and disclose contextual data. Drawing primarily on privacy calculus, with uses-and-gratifications and algorithmic-resistance research specifying benefits and behavioural pathways, this study examines how information-seeking and social presence gratifications relate to adapted resistance-related practices through information privacy concern. We analysed survey data from 719 generative AI users in China using partial least squares structural equation modelling. Both gratifications were positively associated with privacy concern, which was positively associated with self-reported restriction (AAR) and signal-modifying/inference-disrupting (OAR) practices. Information privacy concern statistically accounted for the indirect association between information-seeking gratification and AAR and partially accounted for the other indirect associations. The findings position prompting as a dual information transaction while showing that OAR should not be treated as demonstrated privacy-protective resistance, because prompt variation may also reflect exploratory information seeking or strategic prompt engineering.

documents.abstract: The COVID-19 disruption and subsequent talent mobility exposed important vulnerabilities in traditional service operations. Organizations relying heavily on individual expertise faced risks to operational continuity when experienced professionals moved roles or left. Although knowledge transfer, standard operating procedures, and documentation remain essential, they do not always capture the contextual knowledge developed through years of resolving incidents. The resulting gaps can affect service quality, turnaround time, operating costs, and user experience. This chapter examines how human-AI collaboration can strengthen operational resilience and knowledge continuity in service operations. It draws on the practitioner journey behind IgnitronX.AI, a cloud-native multi-agent platform developed to address enterprise operational challenges using generative AI and agentic AI. Its architecture supports service teams by surfacing similar historical incidents, recommending potential resolutions, enabling knowledge discovery, summarizing operational records, and providing sentiment insights. The objective is not to replace human expertise but to augment it. The implementation journey demonstrated that technology alone cannot deliver sustainable value. Data quality emerged as a critical constraint, alongside security, confidentiality, framework and model selection, operating-cost management, governance, and stakeholder adoption. The experience also reinforced that organizations should first understand the business problem, simplify processes, remove waste, and make deliberate build-versus-buy decisions. Through this reflective practitioner case, the chapter offers leaders practical insights into intelligent operations that preserve organizational knowledge, strengthen service continuity, and create the potential for improved productivity, operational efficiency, and user experience through responsible human-AI collaboration.
